In the beginning. Our wise men taught that the letter bet (of bereshit, in the beginning) is superfluous. They compare it to the bet in the word ba-rishonah (at the first) (Bereshit 13:4). We know the bet in ba-rishonah to be superfluous for we find they shall set forth first (rishonah) (Bamidbar 2:9). However, if this were so the bet (of bereshit) would be vocalized with a long kamatz. Other scholars maintain that the word bereshit is always in the construct and its meaning in our verse is: “In the beginning of the evening, or of the night, or of the darkness.” However, they have overlooked And he chose a first part (reshit) for himself (Devarim 33:21). Others say that the bet of bereshit is a preposition. They explain that Scripture intends to preclude the thought that heaven and earth were preexisting. Hence it states, In the beginning. I believe that bereshit is in the construct, as in In the beginning of (bereshit) the reign of Yehoyakim (Yirmiyahu 26:1). Don’t ask, how can a word in the construct be connected to a verb in the perfect. This presents no problem, for we find that very case in the verse When Hashem spoke at first with Hoshea (Hoshea 1:2), and in the verse the city where David encamped (Yeshayahu 29:1). The meaning of bereshit will be explained in our comments on the next verse.

Created. Most Biblical commentators explain that the word bara (created) indicates creation ex nihilo. But if Hashem make (yivra) a new thing (beri’ah) (Bamidbar 16:30) is similar. However, they have overlooked And Elokim created (va-yivra) the great sea monsters (Bereshit 1:21) and the three times the word created is used in one verse, viz., And Elokim created (va-yivra) man in His own image, in the image of Elokim created (bara) He him; male and female created (bara) He them (Bereshit 1:27). They also failed to consider I form the light, and create darkness (Is. 45:7) wherein darkness, which is the opposite of light, an existing entity, is described by the prophet as being created. The following is the precise explanation of the word bara. Bara has two meanings, one of which has been noted above. The second is found in the verse neither did he eat (bara) bread with them (Shmuel II 12:17). However, in the latter case, an alef has been substituted for a heh. The reason is that bara (in Shmuel I 12:17) is similar to le-havrot (to urge to eat) in And all the people came to cause David to eat (le-havrot) bread (Shmuel II 3:35). The verb le-havrot appears in the hifil (and its root ends with heh), for if it ended with an alef, Scripture would have read le-havri, as in to make yourselves fat (le-havri’achem) with the chiefest of all the offerings of Yisrael (Shmuel I 2:29). We also find bara conjugated in the pi’el, as in and cut down (u-vereta) for thyself (trees) (Yehoshua 17:15). This is not like the similar word beru in choose (beru) you a man for you (Shmuel I 17:8) but rather like bare (hack, dispatch) in and dispatch them (u-vare) with their swords (Yechezkel 23:47). The meaning of bara is to cut or to set a boundary. The intelligent person will understand what I am alluding to.

Elokim. Elokim (Elokim) is a plural. We know this because we come across the singular form Elo’ah. Elokim is employed stylistically. Every language has honorific terminology. In the non-Hebrew tongues when an inferior addresses a superior he employs the plural. In Arabic it is customary for a dignitary such as a king to speak in the plural. In Hebrew, too, it is considered a sign of dignity to employ the plural when speaking of a superior. Such is the case with the words adonim (lords) and be’alim (owners). Thus Scripture says, a cruel lord (adonim) (Is. 19:4), and and the owner thereof (be’alav) shall accept it (Shemot 22:10). The terms alav (upon him), elav (to him), and adav (unto him) are similar. It is for this reason that Scipture reads bara Elokim and not bare’u Elokim. We know from the study of logic that speech is called safah because it is seen to come from the lips. Similarly man’s highest soul is called heart (lev) even though the soul itself is incorporeal while the heart is corporeal. It is referred to in this manner because the heart is its first resting place. Similarly Elokim is called Elokim because His actions are executed via angels who do His will and who are referred to as Elokim. I will explain part of the secret of Elokim’s name when I comment on for My name is in him (Shemot 23:21). Pay no heed to the opinion of Rabbi Saadiah Gaon who holds that man is superior to the angels. I have already explained to you in The Book of Foundation that all of his proofs are wrong. We know that the prophets are the most exalted human beings. Nevertheless, the prophet Yehoshua fell upon his face and prostrated himself before Elokim’s angel and said to him, What saith my lord unto his servant (Yehoshua 5:14). The same is true of the prophets Zecharyah and Daniel. Why should I elaborate when this point is so elementary? The meaning of Hashem of Hosts (Elohe ha-tzeva’ot) is the same as Elokim of gods (Elohe ha-Elokim) (Devarim 10:17). The definition of elohim (lord) is angels. People engaged in the dispensation of Elokim’s justice are also called elohim. Elokim is an adjective, not a proper noun. It is not found conjugated in the perfect or imperfect. One should not assume that angels are composed of fire and air because Scripture states, Who makest winds Thy messengers, The flaming fire Thy ministers (Tehillim 104:4). This is not the literal meaning of this verse. David (in Tehillim 104) speaks first of creation. He starts with light and says, Who coverest Thyself with light as with a garment (Tehillim 104:2). He then goes on to say, Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain, heaven referring to the firmament upon which is water, fire, snow and wind. David next says that the wind serves as Elokim’s agent; i.e., it goes wherever Elokim sends it. He speaks in a similar vein of fire as one of Elokim’s ministers. David then says, Who didst establish the earth upon its foundations (Tehillim 104:5), which refers to dry land. Similarly it is written, Stormy wind, fulfilling His word (Tehillim 148:8).

Et indicates the very thing. It signifies the direct object, as in the heaven (et ha-shamayim). However, sometimes it is omitted, as in that Elokim created man (Devarim 4:32). It is also found placed before the subject, as in and when there came a lion, or (ve-et) a bear (Shmuel I 17:34). However, the latter usage is very rare. Furthermore, et is used in place of with or from.

The heaven. The definite article (ha) is placed before heaven (shamayim) to indicate that Scripture speaks of the heaven visible to man. Heaven (shamayim) is always written in the plural. It is possible that its dominion in Knowest thou the ordinances of the heavens? Canst thou establish its dominion over the earth? (Iyov 38:33) refers to the dominion exercised by each one of the heavenly spheres. The meaning of shamayim (heaven) is high and above, as it is in Arabic, a language akin in form to Hebrew. There is also a heaven of heavens. The word for heaven (shamayim) is never written in the singular. It is like the words millstone (rechayim) and noon (tzohorayim). Those who are well-versed in geometry will understand these secrets. Saadiah Gaon says that the earth may be compared to a point and the heaven to a thread circling it. Since Scripture tells us that heaven and earth were created, we deduce from this that all their contents, such as fire and water, were also created. Others say that the earth includes water and the heaven air. However, in my opinion the heaven and earth spoken of in our verse refer only to the firmament and the dry land. For only one thing was created on each day. Thus light was created on the first day, the firmament on the second, plants on the third, luminaries on the fourth, and living creatures on the fifth and the sixth. This interpretation is borne out by the psalm quoted above (Tehillim 104). It is impossible to maintain that the line circling the dot was created before the dot, or the dot before the circle. Hence our sages say that heaven and earth were created simultaneously. They offer as proof of their viewpoint, Yea, My hand hath laid the foundation of the earth, And My right hand hath spread out the heavens; When I call unto them, They stand up together (Is. 48:13). However, this proof is questionable. The plain meaning of this verse is not so, for how could God address that which was not yet created? How could He call to that which was in a chaotic state? The explanation of this verse is as follows: I, God, created heaven and earth. When I call them, they stand before Me as servants ready to do My will. The meaning of this verse is similar to that of Thy word standeth fast in heaven (Tehillim 119:89). After stating this the Psalmist makes mention of the earth (Tehillim 119:90). He then goes on to say that heaven and earth stand ready to execute any commands that God will direct to them (Tehillim 119:91).

Now the earth. The word ha-aretz (the earth) is irregular in that it is always vocalized with a kamatz beneath both the heh and the alef. It is unlike the word ha-elef (the thousand) in Thou, O Shlomo, shall have the thousand (ha-elef) (Canticles 8:12); or ha-even (the stone) in and this stone (ha-even) (Bereshit 28:22).

Unformed. Saadiah Gaon claims that the word tohu (unformed) is a derivative of tehom (the deep). This explanation is incorrect because the mem of tehom is a root letter like the mem of hadom (footstool). The Sefer Yetzirah explains tohu (unformed) and bohu (void) as follows: Tohu refers to the green line; bohu alludes to the smooth stones. However, the correct meaning of these terms is found in the Aramaic translation of the Pentateuch. We similarly read, And in the waste (tohu), a howling wilderness (Devarim 32:10), and go after vain things (tohu) (Shmuel I 12:21), which means worshipping things that have no substance.

[Void.] Bohu is a synonym of tohu. The vavs of tohu and bohu are in place of a heh. They are like the vav in (va-yishtachu) (and he bowed) and the vav of achu (reed-grass) in They fed in the reed-grass (achu) (Bereshit 41:2). The meaning of our verses is this: When the creation of the firmament and the dry land took place, the earth was uninhabited because it was covered with water. Elokim created the earth in such a way that by the laws of nature it would be below the waters. Do not reject this interpretation because of the vav that is placed before the words the earth (ve-ha-aretz), for its meaning is identical to that of the Arabic fa. The vav placed before the word mist (ed) in but there went up a mist (ve-ed) from the earth (Bereshit 2:6) is analogous. Our verses are to be so interpreted because Moshe did not speak of the eternal world, which is the world of the angels; he spoke only of the transient world. How can those who say that the word heaven in the first verse refers to the highest heavens explain the presence of the earth in the same verse? Intelligent people have reputable proof that there is only one earth. As to the Midrash, when it says that there are seven earths it means that the area of the world inhabited by human beings is divided into seven sections. The Holy Temple was in the center of the inhabited world. It was not in the center of the earth because we know that it was far from there.
And the spirit of Elokim. Ru’ach (wind) is in the construct with Elokim (Hashem) because it was the medium employed by Hashem to dry the land.

[The waters.] Mayim (waters) is in the plural. It does not come in a singular form. It belongs to the dual forms, the latter being either masculine or feminine. Mayim is also found used in the singular in the water of sprinkling was not dashed against him (Bamidbar 19:13).
[Hovered.] Merachefet (hovered) means “blowing above the waters.” As an eagle…Hovereth (yerachef) over her young (Devarim 32:11), is similar.

And Hashem said. Saadiah Gaon interprets va-yomer Elokim (and Hashem said), as and Hashem wanted. However, if this were the case Scripture should have stated Hashem wanted (said) light to be. Therefore va-yomer Elokim is to be rendered “and Hashem said.” We similarly read, By the word of Hashem were the heavens made (Tehillim 33:6), and For He commanded, and they were created (Tehillim 148:5). Scripture describes creation as coming about by Hashem’s word because it wants to teach us that heaven and earth came into being without any labor on Hashem’s part. We may compare this to a king assigning certain tasks to his servants.
[Light.] The light spoken of in this verse was above the air.
And God saw the light. “Saw” is to be understood here as perceived. Compare, Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly (Kohelet 2:13).
The meaning of divided is: He divided them by naming one, day and the other, night.
And God called. The heh of laylah (night) is superfluous, because the word is penultimately accented. It is always a masculine noun.

Evening. Erev (evening) is close in meaning to choshekh (darkness). Erev is so called because forms are then intermingled. The opposite of evening is called boker (morning) because one can then distinguish between various forms. One day refers to the movement of the sphere. There is a secret meaning to the Midrashic statement to the effect that the world will exist for six thousand years. Once it is stated that God called the light “day,” it is impossible to maintain that the evening, too, is considered part of the day.

The correct interpretation of And there was evening and there was morning, one day is that evening passed and the morning of the first day also came. If the intention of this verse is to teach that evening and morning make a day, then what is the meaning of And there was evening and there was morning, a second day (v. 8)?

And God said. Saadiah Gaon says things about the firmament that are not so. The correct interpretation of firmament (raki’a) is something spread out, as in And they did beat (va-yirakke’u) the gold into thin plates (Shemot 39:3); Then did I beat them (erka’em) (Shmuel II 22:43); and similarly, And spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in (Is. 40:22). How precious are the words of he who said that the firmament begins at the point where the sun and the ocean merge. The firmament is the air because when the light shone very strongly upon the earth and a wind dried off from the earth, the flame turned into the firmament. Similarly the Psalmist states, Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain; Who layest the beams of Thine upper chambers in the waters (Tehillim 104:2 and 3). The Psalmist then makes mention of the clouds and the wind and the establishment of the earth. The latter is above the waters. We thus read, For He hath founded it (the earth) upon the seas (Tehillim 24:2), and To Him that spread forth the earth above the waters (Tehillim 136:6). Similarly whoever goes to the ocean is said to be going down. The meaning of (He) That calleth for the waters of the sea, And poureth them out upon the face of the earth (Amos 5:8) is that God commands the waters of the sea to give birth to clouds, and, afterward, And (He) poureth them out upon the face of the earth.

And Elokim made. Dividing one thing from another is expressed by placing the preposition ben (between) before the first object and a lamed before the second, as in And let it divide the waters (ben mayim) from the waters (la-mayim) (Bereshit 1:6) and between the holy (ben kodesh) and the common (le-chol) (Yechezkel 44:23). It may also be expressed by placing the preposition (ben) before each one of the objects, as in our verse and divided the waters (ben ha-mayim) which were under the firmament from the waters (u-ven ha-mayim) which were above the firmament. And it is found with the word ben repeated and a lamed before the second object, as in But your iniquities have separated Between you (benekhem) and your Elokim (le-ven elohekhem) (Is. 59:2).
[And it was so.] This phrase is connected to the verse which follows it: When it was so, God called the firmament heaven.
And Hashem called. There are five things which Hashem named because there was then no man to name them. They are: light, darkness, heaven, earth and the seas. In addition, Hashem named man.

And Elokim said. I believe that this chapter is connected to the one preceding it because the firmament did not come into being until the land dried. Proof of this is Scripture’s statement, In the day that Hashem Elokim made earth (dry land) and heaven (the firmament) (Bereshit 2:4). Thus they were made on the same day. The revelation of something which had previously been hidden (the land) or the gathering of something which was scattered (the water) into one place is not a creation. The meaning of our verse is: now Elokim had said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered. There are hundreds of similar instances in the Torah. I will offer two examples from the portion of Bereshit. One is: And Hashem Elokim planted a garden eastward, in Eden; and there He put the man whom He had formed (Bereshit 2:8). After stating this, Scripture goes on to say, And out of the ground made Hashem Elokim to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight (v. 9). However, Elokim caused vegetation and trees to sprout before the creation of man. The second example is when Elokim commanded man not to eat from the tree of knowledge (Bereshit 2:16). However, immediately after this it is written, And out of the ground Hashem Elokim formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto the man, etc. (Bereshit 2:19). The meaning of formed thus is had formed. According to this interpretation it follows that And Elokim saw that it was good (Bereshit 1:10) is connected to the act of creation which took place on the second day. The account of the creation which took place on the third day thus begins with And Elokim said: Let the earth put forth grass (Bereshit 1:11).

[Let…be gathered.] The meaning of yikkavu is let them come together. Ve-nikvu in At that time they shall call Yerushalayim the throne of the Lord; and all nations shall be gathered (ve-nikvu) unto it (Yirmiyahu 3:17) is similar.
[Seas.] Scripture employs the term seas (yammim) because there is no one name for the sea that surrounds all of the earth.

And Hashem said. Scripture states, Let the earth put forth grass (Bereshit 1:11); Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures (Bereshit 1:20); Let the earth bring forth the living creature after its kind (Bereshit 1:24). This teaches that Hashem placed in the earth and in the water the power to bring forth these things at Hashem’s command. These are the generations (offspring) of the heaven and the earth (Bereshit 2:4).
[Let the earth put forth grass.] Tadshe means let it put forth.
Wherein is the seed thereof. Wherein the seed is in the fruit and each one produces its own kind.

And God said. Yehi (let there be) is short for yiheyeh. Due to the frequency with which this term is used, it is employed before both the singular and the plural. It is also employed in Scripture with the feminine as in, If there be a damsel (yiheyeh) that is a virgin (Devarim 22:23).

For signs and for seasons. For signs, i.e., for minutes, and for seasons, i.e., for hours. For signs may also be interpreted as referring to the eclipse of the moon and the sun and also to shooting stars. The last-mentioned phenomena are to be included among the signs produced by the lights of the firmament because they are caused by the stars. This meaning of signs is like signs in And be not dismayed at the signs (omens) of heaven (Yirmiyahu 10:2). Anyone who explains the lamed of le-otot (for signs) as superfluous is mistaken.

And let them be for signs. A prominent Spanish sage stated that the firmament is divided into eight parts, seven for the seven spheres of the seven stars and one for the constellations. However, this cannot be so because we know there is no body above the sphere of the constellations. Behold, Scripture explicitly states, And God set them in the firmament of the heaven, which clearly indicates that there is a heaven above the firmament. The heaven of heavens (Nechemyah 9:6) and To Him that rideth upon the heaven of heavens, which are of old (kedem) (Tehillim 68:34) are similar. Note that the word kedem in the verse quoted above does not mean east but ancient. Indeed, Rabbi Saadiah Gaon, may the righteous be remembered for a blessing, was afraid to comment on this verse. It appears to me that the sun, the moon and other luminaries are called lights in the firmament because they are visible there.

And God made. The sun and the moon are called the great lights in contradistinction to the stars. Similarly the first three sons of Yishai are called the elders, in contrast to their younger brothers. In reality, Eliav, the first born, was the oldest of them all. As to the Midrash, which states One was not greater than the other, there is a secret meaning to it.

[To rule the day.] The sun rules during the day and not at night because it is not seen. Conversely, the light of the moon and stars are not seen during the day. One may ask, do not the astronomers teach that Jupiter and all the stars, with the exception of Mercury and Venus, are larger than the moon? Why, then, is it written the great lights? The answer is that the term great does not refer to size but to light, and the light of the moon is many times greater than their light because of its proximity to the earth. Thus we see that Scripture describes them as lights.
And God set. Do not be surprised that Scripture states, And God set, for the Bible also says, I have set My bow in the cloud (Bereshit 9:13).

And to rule. The day spoken of in the Torah begins at sunrise and lasts until sunset. Night begins when the stars are first visible. Those who say that night begins with the appearance of three stars are correct. Know that evening begins at sunset and lasts for one and a third hours, during which time a light-like appearance is seen in the clouds. Similarly morning dawns before sunrise. When the light of the sun shines during the day and the light of the moon at night, they separate between the light and the dark.

And God said. Yishritzu (let it swarm) is a transitive verb, as is sharatz (swarm) in And the river shall bring forth swarms of frogs (ve-sharatz) (Shemot 7:28). The meaning of Let the waters bring forth swarms of living creatures and let fowl fly above the earth is that the waters shall produce living beings that will immediately fly. The verse And let fowl fly…in the open firmament of heaven proves my interpretation of the firmament. Saadiah Gaon explains al pene (in the open) to mean with the face of. Hence, according to the Gaon, the heavens face down. The feh of ye’ofef (let fly) is doubled like the nun in yekhonen (till He establish) (Is. 62:7).
And God created. The meaning of romeset (creepeth) is walks. Some are of the opinion that the sin of romeset is in place of a samekh.

And God blessed. The meaning of Be fruitful, and multiply is, “You shall be fruitful and you shall multiply.” And die in the mount (Devarim 32:50) is similar because it is not in one’s power to determine the time of one’s death.
And God said. Living creature is a general term for what the fire, water and earth gave birth to. It also includes man.
Cattle. Domesticated beasts that are utilized by man for their needs, for riding and for food.
And creeping thing. Small animals that walk upon the earth.

And beast of the earth. Animals that are in the wilderness where there are no human settlements. The vav at the end of ve-chayeto (and beast of) is superfluous. It is like the vav of le-mayeno (into a fountain) in into a fountain (le-mayeno) of waters (Tehillim 114:8), and the vav in the son of (beno) Beor (Bamidbar 24:3).

Let us make man. Some are of the opinion that na’aseh (let us make) is a nifal participle and is to be compared to the same word in Now that which was prepared (na’aseh) for one day (Nechemyah 5:18). They further say that in our image, after our likeness are the words of Moshe. They also explain the pronominal suffix “his” in And Elokim created man in His own image (v. 27) as referring to man, and connect Elokim (in Bereshit 9:6) to made rather than to image. They read this verse as follows: “For Elokim made man in an image,” rather than “for in the image of Elokim made He man.” Now this interpretation is absurd. According to it the first quoted verse should have read, “Let a man be made.” Similarly Scripture should have read, “He made him in his image.” Furthermore, how can the his in His image (v. 27) refer to man? If this were the case then man had an image before he was created. Finally, what sense would there be to Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed (Bereshit 9:6), if the reason for the above is that man was made in an image? All living things have an image. Saadiah Gaon explains in our image, after our likeness as referring to the dominion man exercises on earth. He explains His image as the image that Elokim in His wisdom chose for man because He saw that this image was good for man. The Gaon further notes that Scripture connects image to Elokim (be-tzelem Elokim) to stress man’s glorified state. Similarly Scripture states, and are gone forth out of His land (Yechezkel 36:20). The Bible says this to emphasize the importance of the land of Yisrael because, in reality, The earth is Hashem’s, and the fullness thereof (Tehillim 24:1). The Gaon also says that the word na’aseh (let us make) has the meaning of the singular even though it is in the plural because it is the plural of majesty. He offers as proof, and we will give thee the other also (Bereshit 29:27); and we will tell the interpretation thereof before the king (Daniel 2:36); peradventure I shall prevail, that we may smite (nakkeh) them (Bamidbar 22:6). However, these witnesses are false witnesses. First of all, and we will give thee (ve-nittenah) (Bereshit 29:27) is a nifal and its meaning is “the other will also be given thee.” It is like the word nittenah (is given) in and the city is given (nittenah) (Yirmiyahu 32:24). The vav conversive changes nittenah (she was given) to “she will be given (ve-nittenah),” as is the case with every verb in the perfect which becomes an imperfect when a vav conversive is prefixed to it. Similarly nakkeh bo (we may smite them) (Bamidbar 22:6) means, “I and my army will smite them.” Further, nakkeh may be a pi’el infinitive meaning to smite, like nakeh (destroy) in But will not utterly destroy thee (ve-nakkeh lo anakkekah) (Yirmiyahu 46:28). The latter interpretation is supported by the fact that Scripture employs the phrase lo nukku (were not smitten) (Shemot 9:32), and a verb cannot come in the pu’a l unless it also comes in the pi’el. Rabbi Moshe Ha-kohen, the Spaniard, errs in his book. Similarly we will tell (Daniel 2:36) is Aramaic. For if we will tell is a plural of majesty, how would Daniel dare to speak in such haughty terms before Nevuchadnetzar who was the “King of Kings”?I will now explain. Note that all the works of creation came into being by Elokim’s command for the sake of man. Scripture relates that the earth and water brought forth plants and all living creatures. After all plants and living creatures had been created, Elokim said to the angels, Let us make man; i.e., We, rather than the earth and water, will occupy ourselves with his creation. We know that the Torah spoke the language of man, for it was given to humans who speak and hear. Now a human being cannot speak of things above or below him without employing human terminology. Hence Scripture uses such terms as the mouth of the earth (Bamidbar 16:30), the hand of the Yarden (Bamidbar 13:29), and the head of the dust of the world (Mishlei 8:26). Far be it from us to believe that Elokim has an image. Scripture clearly refutes such a notion by stating, To whom then will you liken Me, that I should be equal (Is. 40:25). It is because man’s upper soul is eternal and is compared in its existence to Elokim and because man’s soul is incorporeal and fills the body, which is a microcosm, in the same way that Elokim fills the universe that Scripture states, in our image, after our likeness. May Elokim’s name be blessed. He commenced with the macrocosm and concluded with the microcosm. The prophet also says that he saw Elokim’s glory appear in human form (Yechezkel 1:26). Elokim is one. He is the creator of all. He is all. I cannot explain further. Man was originally created with two faces; man is thus one but also two. In the image of Elokim means in the image of the angels. Man was created both male and female. The words Be fruitful, and multiply are a blessing not a command, just as they are with regard to the creatures brought forth by the waters (Bereshit 1:22). Nevertheless, there is in fact a commandment to be fruitful and multiply transmitted by our sages, of blessed memory, which they attached to this verse in order to remember the commandment.

And Elokim said: behold I have given you. Elokim permitted mankind and every living thing to eat all herbs. He also permitted man to eat the fruits of the trees and limited the animals and creeping things to green herbs. At this point in time the consumption of flesh was not permitted. That came after the flood.

The sixth day. Some say that the word yom (day) is in the construct with sixth, and the meaning of yom ha-shishi (the sixth day) is the day of the sixth sphere. They say the same with regard to yom ha-shevi’i (the seventh day). However, they are wrong. Proof of their error is found in the teaching of the astrologers who tell us who the lord of the sixth day is. The meaning of yom ha-shishi, then, is the sixth day from day one. This is also the meaning of the seventh day. We similarly find ish ha-yisraeli (the Yisraeli man) (Vayikra 24:10) and many such cases, among them reki’a ha-shamayim (Bereshit 1:20), which should be rendered as “the firmament which is heaven.”

Were finished. Va-yekhullu is a pu’al. It follows the paradigm of va-yekhussu (were covered) in and all the high mountains…were covered (Bereshit 7:19). Its meaning is: were finished. The earth includes the oceans since they form one entity.

And on the seventh day Elokim finished. Some say that the days are created entities, and with the creation of the seventh day Elokim’s work was finished. However, this interpretation is unpalatable. Others say that the bet may indicate before, as in Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out (be-disho) the corn (Devarim 25:4), and in howbeit the first day (ba-yom ha-rishon) ye shall put away leaven out of your houses (Shemot 12:15). However, why go through all this trouble when finishing work does not constitute an act. Saying Elokim finished is equivalent to saying Elokim did no work. This is the meaning of Elokim finished and of and He rested.
His work which He had made refers to the work that he had done on Friday prior to the onset of the Sabbath.
And He rested on the seventh day from all His work pertains to all creations that God brought into being.

And Elokim blessed. A blessing means an increase in well being. On the Sabbath the body is blessed with a renewal of its reproductive strength and the soul with an increase in its intellectual and reasoning capabilities.
And hallowed it. No work was done on the Sabbath, in contrast to the other six days.

[Which Elokim in creating had made.] Its meaning is: Elokim placed in the root of all the species the power to reproduce themselves. I disagree with the person who explains la’asot (had made) as having the same meaning as made and who, furthermore, insists that created and made are synonymous. Saadiah Gaon explains that the blessing and the holiness spoken of in this verse refer to those who observe the Sabbath. They will be blessed and sanctified.
These are the generations. These are what they gave birth to.
When they were created. When the firmament came into being and the earth became visible.

[In the day that the Lord God made.] Be-yom asot means in the day that God fixed. Proof of this can be seen in and He hastened to dress it (la-asot oto) (Bereshit 18:7), and in Whom I have created which is then followed by I have formed him, and finally by yea, I have made him (asitiv) (Is. 43:7).

Shrub. Si’ach (shrub) means a tree: so, too, in Among the bushes (sichim) they bray (Iyov 30:7). In my opinion si’ach refers to a fruit-bearing tree, because Scripture compares man to a tree. Behold, Scripture employs such terms as tree (si’ach), fruit, bough, limb, top of a tree and branch when speaking of man.

A mist. Ed (mist) means smoke. The day of their calamity (yom edom) is similar (Devarim 32:35). An evil day is called a cloudy day and a day of thick darkness. The meaning of our verse is that via the power of the lights a mist arose from the earth and watered it and caused it to bring forth vegetation. Saadiah Gaon explains as follows: “And no mist yet went up from the earth.”
Then the Lord God formed. Via the power of the lights.
[Formed.] Va-yitzer (formed) is a kal. It belongs to those verbs whose first root letter is a yod. It is like va-yiketz in And Noach awoke (va-yiketz no’ach) (Bereshit 9:24).

The meaning of and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life is that man lives through the nostrils. They remove the air heated by the heart and replace it with fresh air. Scripture says man became nefesh chayyah (a living soul) because like the animals he was immediately able to walk, and thus differed from babies subsequently born.

And the Lord Elokim planted. Elokim had previously planted a garden in the eastern section of the world in a place called Eden. He now placed the man there. The bet of be-eden (in Eden) in in Eden the garden of Elokim (Yechezkel 28:13) governs not only Eden but also garden. Its meaning thus is, in Eden, in the garden of Elokim. Even by the Elokim (me’el) of thy father, who shall help thee and by (ve-et) the Almighty, who shall bless thee (Bereshit 49:25) is similar. There are many other such instances in Scripture.

[The man.] There is a secret meaning as to why the definite article has been placed in front of Adam. The definite article is also found prefixed to Menashe in the half tribe of Menashe (shevet ha-menasheh) (Devarim 3:13) and before the word Aravnah in of Aravnah the Yevusi (Shmuel II 24:16). It is also possible that the definite article is placed before Adam because the word adam is derived from the word used for ground (adamah). Hence the name Adam may be a proper name or an adjective.

And out of the ground made the Lord to grow. When God made the trees grow from the ground throughout the world he did the same in the Garden of Eden, but there he placed two trees not found anywhere else in the world.

And the tree of the knowledge. In my opinion the phrase and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is to be understood as if written, “And the tree of the knowledge, knowledge of good and evil,” because the word knowledge has a definite article prefixed to it and thus cannot be in the construct. The ark of the covenant (Yehoshua 3:14) and even the prophecy of Oded the prophet (Divrei Hayamim II 15:8) are similar. There are many other similar instances in Scripture.
And a river. Before man was created the river watered the garden on all sides.
[Heads.] The alef in the word roshim (heads) is a root letter. In marashotekhem (headtires) (Yirmiyahu 13:18) the alef is enunciated. The meaning of marashotekhem is your headtires.

The name of the first. Saadiah Gaon identifies Pishon with the Yeor. But it is known that the Gichon is close to the land of Yisrael, for Scripture states, And bring him (Shlomo)…down to Gichon…and…anoint him there king over Yisrael (Melachim I 1:33,34). It (the Gichon) flows from southeast of the land of Yisrael. The same is true of the Perat (Perat), which marks the furthermost eastern boundary of the land of Yisrael. The commentaries also tell us that the Chidekel (Chiddekel) is another river, in addition to the Perat, that flows through Baghdad. Thus these three rivers (the Gichon, the Perat and the Chidekel) lie east of the land of Yisrael. Furthermore, the source of the Yeor is in the mountain of Frankincense far south of the equator. Proof of this can be seen by the fact that its waters swell in the summer. We know that the Garden of Eden is below the equator where day and night are always equal. Fools question this and ask, how is this possible? However, there is positive proof that this is so. Thus according to Saadiah one must believe that the Pishon (the Yeor) flows from the Garden of Eden, which is in the east, toward the mountain of Frankincense, which is in the southwest, and then flows north. There is, in fact, no proof that the Pishon is the Yeor. Indeed, Saadiah translates the land of Chavilah which the Pishon compasses to fit in with his translation of the Pishon as being the Yeor. The fact of the matter is that he had no tradition concerning these things. He did the same with families, states, animals, fowl and precious stones. Perhaps these things were revealed to him in a dream. He definitely erred in a number of them as I will point out in their proper place. So we will not rely on his dreams. Perhaps he did so out of respect for the honor of Hashem, for he translated the Torah into Arabic language and script and he did not want the Arvim to think that there are parts of Scripture which we do not understand. Scripture mentions that there is gold in the land of Chavilah in order to glorify the river coming out of the Garden of Eden.

And the gold. Saadiah Gaon renders bedolach (bedellium) as pearls. He compares manna to them. However, Scripture merely says that manna had the color of bedolach (Bamidbar 11:7). The Gaon also says that shoham (onyx) is a precious clear white stone. The fact of the matter is that we do not know the precise meaning of either of these two items.

[Toward the east of Ashur.] The tav of kidmat (toward the east of) is in place of a heh. The difference between kedem and kedemah is that the heh suffixed to kedemah is in place of the preposition “to” (el), which is vocalized with a segol. Similarly in and Avram went down into Mitzrayim (mitzraymah) (Bereshit 12:10), mitzraymah means “to Mitzrayim.” Kidmat asshur thus means toward the east of Ashur. Note that from the first verse of the Torah until the word made (Bereshit 2:3), Scripture refers to the Deity as Elokim. Afterward, the honored and revered name (the Tetragrammaton) is coupled with it. How precious are the words of the ancients of blessed memory who said that the complete name of God is used over a complete world. Prior to the completion of creation there was no power to receive this name. If God grants me life I will explain the secret of the Tetragrammaton when I comment upon the first Torah portion of the book of Shemot. I will then explain its meaning in the absolute and in the construct. Note that the location of the ground from which Adam was created was close to the Garden of Eden. I note this because some say that Adam was created out of the ground of the land of Yisrael. They have overlooked And it came to pass, as they journeyed east (Bereshit 11:2).

Into the garden of Eden. Gan (garden) can be both masculine and feminine, hence the plurals gannim and gannot. We ask those who maintain that the words to till (dress) it and to keep it (le-ovdah u-le-shomrah) refer to the ground (adamah), how it is possible to till and keep a large area from a small one. Furthermore, after Adam sinned God expelled him from the garden and commanded him to till the soil. But according to their interpretation he was already tilling the soil while he was living in the Garden of Eden.

To till it (le-ovdah) therefore refers to the garden of whose fruit he ate. It was only after he sinned that he had to eat the grass of the ground, i.e., bread. To till it means to water it. To keep it means to guard the garden so that no animals enter therein and befoul it. Some say that le-ovdah means to serve God’s commandment. However, a commandment is not served.

And the Lord God commanded the man. The verb tzivvah (command) with the preposition al (upon) implies a prohibition. We similarly read, I will also command (atzavveh) the clouds (al he-avim) That they rain no rain upon it (Is. 5:6).

[Thou shalt not eat of it.] Even though I (Hashem) permitted you to eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden, do not eat of the fruit of the tree of knowledge. One might ask, What need is there for the term of it after having stated but of the tree of the knowledge…thou shalt not eat? The answer is that the Bible elaborates. We find a similar case in And she opened it, and saw it, even the child (Shemot 2:6). It is also possible that the term of it means even a part of it. You will find the exact grammatical explanation of the term mi-mennu (of it) in the Sefer ha-yisod. Note that Adam was an intelligent being, for Hashem would not direct commands to one who was unintelligent. He was deficient in the knowledge of good and evil of only one thing. Don’t you see that Adam named every animal and fowl according to the nature of each of their respective species? Thus he was extremely intelligent. If Adam was unintelligent, Hashem, knowing this, would not have brought His creatures to him to see what name he would give to each one of them. Hashem also showed Adam the tree of knowledge, for his wife knew that it was in the midst of the garden.
And the Lord God said. It is not good means it is not good for the man.
A help meet. Help meet should be understood in the light of Two are better than one (Kohelet 4:9).

[Whatsoever the man would call.] The lamed (to) in the clause and whatsoever the man would call also applies to the phrase living creature. Our clause is to be read as follows: and whatsoever the man would call to it, to every living creature, that was to be the name thereof. The verse elaborates, as in And she opened it, and saw it, even the child (Shemot 2:6). There are many other such instances.

[To all cattle.] Le-khol (to all) also governs two words, for the meaning of our verse is: And the man gave names to all cattle, and to all the fowl of the air. In that his men become few (Devarim 33:6) and And I have not learned wisdom (Mishlei 30:3) are similar. There are many other such instances.

[But for Adam.] The meaning of but for Adam he did not find a help meet is that Adam did not find a helpmeet for himself. This is the way of the Hebrew language. Thus we find Shmuel saying, And Hashem sent Yeruba'al, and Bedan, and Yiftach, and Shmuel (Shmuel I 12:11). It appears farfetched to me that he did not find a help meet refers to Hashem. Scripture says here that the fowl were created out of the ground. However, it states above that they were created out of the water. This is so because the fowl were created out of both earth and water.
And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall. Va-yappel (caused to fall) is a hifil, as is va-yashev (drove away) in and Avram drove them away (Bereshit 15:11).
A deep sleep. Tardemah is a deeper sleep than shenah, and shenah is a deeper sleep than tenumah. The tav of tardemah (deep sleep) is not part of its root.
One of his ribs. Adam had two sides. Tzela here is like tzela (side) in and for the second side (tzela) of the tabernacle (Shemot 26:20). Tzela is a feminine noun. It means a side.

Instead thereof. Tachtennah means in its place. Tachtennah (instead thereof) spelled with a superfluous nun is in the singular. Tachtehah is its plural form. Tachteni (under me) and tachtai (under me) are similar.
Made he. Va-yiven (made me) is a hifil conjugation. We find similar instances with the kal conjugation in va-yifen (and he turned) (Shemot 7:23) and va-yiken (and he bought) (Bereshit 33:19).

And brought her. When Adam awoke from his sleep he thought that the woman was brought before him as the animals were brought before him. Scripture speaks of Adam’s thoughts. Similarly, And the men pursued after them (Yehoshua 2:7). It is also possible that the woman was created outside of the garden and then was brought to Adam. When he looked around he knew that she had been cut from him, for one of his sides with its flesh was missing and he felt that it had been closed with other flesh.
And the man said. Then Adam said, “This time I have found a help meet like me for me, for this being came out of me.” The tradition concerning Lilith is a homily.
Le-zot (she) means because of this. Say of me: (li) He is my brother (Bereshit 20:13) is similar.

[Woman.] The shin in the word ishah (woman) receives a dagesh in place of the inaudible yod which is found in the word ish (man). However, it is possible that ishah (woman) receives a dagesh to distinguish it from ishah (her husband) for at times the dagesh in the suffixed pronominal heh in ishah (her husband) is not pronounced. The plural nashim (women) is derived from the words enosh (man) and anashim (men).
[Shall be called.] This refers to the name of the woman.

[She was taken.] The dagesh is omitted in the kof of lukachah (she was taken) in order to simplify its enunciation. This word is a pu’al conjugation even though we do not find it conjugated in the pi’el.

[And they shall be one flesh.] This means they shall live together as if they were one flesh, or let them once again be one flesh. Some say they will be one flesh through the child they will produce. However, this interpretation is farfetched.

Naked. Arummim (naked) is an adjective. And stripped the naked (arummim) of their clothing (Iyov 22:6) is similar. Some say that arum (prudent) in A prudent man (arum) seeth the evil and hideth himself (Mishlei 22:3) has essentially the same meaning. What the verse means is that the mind of the wise is uncovered (arum) and open to everything like the eye.

And were not ashamed. Yitboshashu (ashamed) is related to the word boshet (shame). It is an ayin, vav. The last letter of the root is doubled. It is like the verb yitbonen (he will consider) (Iyov 11:11). A kamatz is placed beneath the first shin because the word ends a verse.

Now the serpent. Some say that the woman understood and knew the language of the animals. They interpret And the serpent said as meaning, that the serpent spoke through signs. Others say that the serpent was in reality Satan. Now why don’t they look at what Scripture states at the close of this chapter (v. 14 and 15)? How is Satan to crawl upon his belly or eat the dust of the ground? Furthermore, what meaning is there to the curse they shall bruise thy head if the reference is to Satan? Many err and inquire why the serpent was cursed. They ask, was the serpent fully intelligent? Was he commanded by Hashem to refrain from beguiling the woman? Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says since we know that only humans are intelligent and capable of speaking, we must conclude that neither the serpent nor Bilam’s ass spoke. He argues that in reality an angel spoke for them. However, Rabbi Shmuel ben Hofni took issue with him. On the other hand, Rabbi Shlomo ibn Gabirol, the great Spanish scholar and poet who wrote metered verse, arose and disagreed with Rabbi Shmuel ben Hofni. It appears to me that we are to interpret the account of the serpent literally. The serpent spoke and walked in an upright position. The One who gave intelligence to man also gave it to the serpent. Scripture itself bears witness that the serpent, although not as intelligent as man, was more subtle (arum) than any beast of the field. The meaning of arum (subtle) is wise, i.e., one who conducts his affairs intelligently. Now do not be surprised that Scripture uses the term arum (subtle, in v. 1) after arummim (naked in Bereshit 2:25) when each of these words has a different meaning. Scripture is being poetic. Similarly, With the jawbone of an ass (ha-chamor), heaps upon heaps (chamor chamoratayim) (Shoftim 15:16), and on thirty ass colts (ayarim), and they had thirty cities (ayarim) (Jud. 10:4). Furthermore, if an angel spoke via the mouth of the serpent, then the serpent did not sin. This angel could not be Hashem’s messenger. Neither does an angel rebel against Hashem. Those who ask, how did the serpent find the woman, are not asking a valid question.

The use of the term af ki (yea) shows that the serpent spoke other things to the woman and that at the end of his conversation with her said, “yea much more so (af ki) now that Hashem said: Ye shall not eat of any tree of the garden (v. 1).”The serpent did not mention the revered and feared name of Hashem because he did not know it. The woman also added to Hashem’s commandment, neither shall ye touch it. The wife of Manoach did the same when she quoted the angel as saying, for the child shall be a Nazirite unto Hashem from the womb to the day of his death (Jud. 13:7).
And ye shall be as Elokim. As angels.
And when the woman saw. In her heart.
And that the tree was to be desired. Because it had the power to make one wise, and her eyes would “open.”

[Unto her husband with her.] The meaning of with her is that they ate together of the fruit and that she disclosed to him the secret that the serpent had revealed to her. Adam thus did not sin unwittingly and was therefore punished for violating God’s command. Many commentators say that the tree of knowledge was a fig tree. They base their assertion on and they sewed fig-leaves together, and made themselves girdles (v. 7). However, if this interpretation were correct, the Bible would say, “And they sewed leaves of the tree of the knowledge.” Many others say that it was a wheat plant. However, in my opinion the two trees in the midst of the garden were unique species not found anywhere else on the face of the earth. One of them, the tree of knowledge, possessed the power to instill sexual desire. Therefore the man and woman covered their nakedness. The meaning of va-yitperu (sewed) is well-known. Tafarti in I have sewed (tafarti) sackcloth upon my skin (Iyov 16:15) is similar. Those who ask where Adam and Chavah got a needle (to sew their girdle) emit hot air. Adam and Chavah could have used a sharp piece of wood. Upon eating of the tree of knowledge, Adam knew (yada) his wife. Yada (knew) is a euphemism for sexual intercourse. Sexual intercourse is called “knowledge” because sexual desire came from the tree of knowledge. Moreover, a young man begins to have sexual desire at the age at which he begins to “know” good and evil.

The tree of life extended life so that by partaking of it man would live for many years. Le-olam (v. 22) does not mean forever. We find this to be the case with the term olam in and he shall serve him for ever (le-olam) (Shemot 21:6), and in and there abide for ever (Shmuel I 1:22) and in many other verses,Some commentators insist that the verse for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die (Bereshit 2:17) indicates that man was created immortal and that he became mortal as a punishment for his sin. Many ask, what sin did Adam’s children commit that they were punished with death? Now this is absurd. Man and beast both share a common spirit (life force) through which they live and experience sensations in this world. As animals are destined to die, so must man die. The advantage of man over beast lies in the portion from above (the soul) which man has been granted. A Greek physician has proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that it is impossible for man to live forever.

And they heard the voice of Hashem Hashem walking. They heard the voice of Hashem walking toward evening, at the time of the day when the breeze blows. Scripture employs the term holekh (walking) when referring to a voice as seen in The sound thereof shall go (yelekh) like the serpent’s (Yirmiyahu 46:22), and And when the voice of the horn waxed (holekh) louder and louder (Shemot 19:19). However, the Spanish grammarian, Rabbi Yonah ibn Janah, says that this verse is to be interpreted as follows: And they heard the voice of Hashem as man was walking in the garden. He also interprets the day referred to in for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die (Bereshit 2:17) as meaning a thousand years, as the Midrash does. Others say that Adam was created on a Friday and died on a Friday. Others say that the meaning of for in the day…thou shalt surely die is that on that day you will incur the death penalty. Still others say that die at times means punishment, as seen in the verse the man that hath done this deserveth to die (Shmuel II 12:5). Still others say the meaning of this verse is that on the day you eat of this tree you will begin to die. They bring proof from a child. According to my thinking the correct interpretation of this verse is to be found in the words of the Rabbinic sages who said that Adam repented. Their interpretation is in keeping with the words of Yirmiyahu who says, At one instant I may speak concerning a nation…to destroy it, but if that nation turn from their evil.. J repent of the evil that I thought to do unto it (Yirmiyahu 18:7, 8).

And Hashem Hashem called. Where art thou was a means of starting a conversation. Similarly, Where is Hevel thy brother? (Bereshit 4:9). Behold, Kayin denied his brother’s whereabouts, but Hashem responded, the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto Me from the ground (Bereshit 4:10).
Shouldest not. Bilti with a lamed prefixed to it (le-vilti) means “not to.” Without this lamed (bilti) it means “only.”
Eat. Akhol (eat) is an infinitive. It is like shemor (keep) in in not keeping (shemor) His commandments (Devarim 8:11).

Whom thou gavest to be with me. Thou gavest to me one who gave me the fruit to eat. The word immadi (to be with me) means the same as immi (with me). Its meaning is: to be with me in the garden. However, immadi, in contradistinction to immi, is found only in the first person singular.

And I did eat. The alef of va-okhel (and I did eat) is a first person imperfect prefix. Its vowel (a cholam) takes the place of the alef of the root that has been dropped. The khaf is vocalized with a tzere because and I did eat comes at the end of a verse. A vav prefixed to a participle is always vocalized with a sheva, and never with a kamatz.
Beguiled me. Persuaded me.
Cursed. The serpent was cursed with a short life. However, the correct interpretation is that the serpent was cursed in manner of locomotion.

Upon thy belly. Gechonekha (thy belly) means thy chest. We cannot determine if the nun of gakhon (thy belly) is part of the root of this word, as the nun of adon (lord) is, or if it is a paradigm nun like the nun of zadon (insolence). Those who say that gakhon is so called because of the air that rushes forth from it are indulging in homiletics. They similarly explain Gichon (Bereshit 2:13). They also say that Pishon (Bereshit 2:11) comes from the same root as tafushu (ye gambol) in Because ye gambol (tafushu) as a heifer (Yirmiyahu 50:11). Also, they say that Perat (the Perat, Bereshit 2:14) comes from the same roots as Be fruitful (peru), and multiply (u-revu) (Bereshit 1:28). But they are unable to cross the great river, the Chiddeckel (the Chidekel) (Bereshit 1:28), which stood before them. They decided that it is made up of two words, chad (swift) and kal (light), and means the river whose waters are swift and light.

And I will put enmity…they shall bruise thy head. Her children shall smite thee upon thy head. Yeshufeni (bruise) in He that would break me (yeshufeni) with a tempest (Iyov 9:17) is similar to yeshufekha (shall bruise thee). Look at what follows and you will see that it is so. A bet has been omitted from the word rosh (head) in they shall bruise thy head. We find the same in into the house (bet) of Hashem (Melachim II 12:17).
Heel. Ekev means the foot. If the head symbolizes the first, then the heel symbolizes the last. Akevo in their rear (akevo) lying in wait on the west (Yehoshua 8:13), is similar.
I will greatly multiply. Harbah (multiply) is an infinitive.
Thy pain. The pain a woman suffers when she is deflowered.
And thy travail. The nun of ve-heronekh (and thy travail) is not a root letter. Pregnancy is considered by our verse to be a punishment because it and childbirth are a burden to women.
Thy desire. Thy obedience. This means you will obey whatever your husband commands you for you are under his authority to do his will.
And unto Adam…cursed is the ground. It will not yield much produce.
In toil thou shalt eat of it. This is short for thou shalt eat of its produce. And let them be of those that eat at thy table (Melachim I 2:7) is similar.
Thorns also and thistles. Kotz refers to large thorns. Dardar (thistles) are smaller than thorns. Its root is dalet, resh (dar). The other two letters of the word are not root letters.
[In toil.] Thou shalt toil in opening, harrowing and sowing. In addition to this, man will also suffer the sick evil of finding thorns growing amidst the produce of the field.
[The herb of the field.] Bread. For prior to this, man sustained himself with the fruits of the Garden of Eden.

[In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread]. Unlike the animals, you will have to work at winnowing, grinding, kneading and cooking before you can eat. The meaning of ze’at (sweat of) can be ascertained from Rabbinic sources. It follows the paradigm of shenah (sleep). Its root is yod, zayin, ayin. Ba-yazah in they shall not gird themselves with anything that causeth sweat (ba-yazah) (Yechezkel 44:18) is similar. The meaning of the verse is, they shall not come to sweat. We know that man is created out of the four elements. What, then, does Scripture mean by for out of it (dust) was thou taken? The answer is that man’s skeletal frame is created out of earth (dust). Hence the bones are heavy and lack sensation. The skeletal frame is the foundation of the body. Look, Scripture states, and the bones came together, bone to its bone (Yechezkel 37:7). The bones are like the frame of a house. Thus after the bones came together and, lo, there were sinews upon them, and flesh came up, and skin covered them above (Yechezkel 37:8). Similarly Scripture states, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence (Bereshit 50:25).

Chavah. The yod and vav are interchangeable. We thus find hoyah and hoveh interchanged in behold, the hand of Hashem is upon (hoyah) thy cattle (Shemot 9:3), and in and thou wouldest be (hoveh) be their king (Nechemyah 6:6). The reason she was called Chavvah and not Chayyah is to distinguish her name from the noun meaning animal (chayyah).
The mother of all living. Humans.

Garments of skin. Some say that Adam and Chavah originally consisted of bone and flesh, and Hashem now covered them with skin. Others say garments of skin means garments for their skin. Still others say that there exists an animal which has a form similar to that of man, and Hashem commanded that it shed its skin. However, one should in reality not bother to inquire into this matter. We ought to believe that Hashem made garments of skin for Adam and Chavah. Who can recount all of Hashem’s mighty acts? Who can tell of all of his wonders? There is no end to Hashem’s greatness.

And the Lord God said…as one of us. When one (echad) is in the absolute, it has a cantillical note which indicates the foregoing and it is vocalized with a segol beneath the alef. However, when it is vocalized with a pattach beneath the alef (achad) it is in the construct. Similarly, As one of (ke-achad) the tribes of Yisrael (Bereshit 49:16). Hence, according to the rules of grammar, the word ke-achad (as one of) cannot have the meaning of as one. Additionally, if ke-achad is in the absolute, then it is meaningless. Furthermore, if ke-achad is in the absolute, the notes should have connected mi-mennu (of us) to la-da’at (to know). Mi-mennu is a plural,

The word mi-mennu can be rendered of us or of him. as in ish mi-mennu (none of us) (Bereshit 23:6). I have already explained in The Book of Foundation why the nun of mi-mennu receives a dagesh when in the plural. The Babylonian grammarians who do not place a dagesh in it are in error. The meaning of the verse (v. 22) is the same as ye shall be as God, knowing good and evil (v. 5). On the other hand, God might be saying what was in Adam’s mind. The use of the term of us presents no problem. It is similar to Let us make man in our image (Bereshit 1:26) and Come, let us go down (Bereshit 11:7). God in all these cases is addressing the angels.

Therefore the Lord God sent him forth. When the word shelach (sent forth) is followed by a mem, it has a negative connotation and means banished, as in cast them out (shalach) of My sight (Yirmiyahu 15:1). The great Spanish scholar who interpreted sent him forth in our verse in a positive way, as in and Avraham went with them to bring them (le-shallecham) on the way (Bereshit 18:16), and in and he hath sent him away (va-yeshallechehu), and he is gone in peace (Shmuel II 3:23), erred. For if he was right then the place Adam was going to was a better place than the Garden of Eden. If this sage should ask, if the meaning of sent him forth is he banished him, then why does Scripture go on to say, So He drove out the man (v. 24)? The answer is that when man was driven from the garden (v. 4), God placed the cherubim at the east of the Garden of Eden.

[The cherubim.] Some say that cherubim means like images of youths, which is the translation of the Aramaic ke-ravyah. However, I believe that the word is a general term for any image. Yechezkel, who first says that he saw the image of an ox (Yechezkel 1:10) and later speaks of a cherub (Yechezkel 10:14), refers to one and the same image. The image was not changed from that of an ox to that of a cherub because an ox would be a reminder of the sin of the golden calf, as this sin was not committed in Yechezkel’s day. When Yechezkel speaks of the cherub (10:14) he has in mind the image he had mentioned previously (the image of an ox in 1:10). Therefore every image of an ox is a cherub, but not every cherub is an image of an ox. Proof of this is that Yechezkel refers to all images that he had seen as cherubim (10:20). Our verse speaks of the cherubim, which implies the cherubim known to all, i.e., angels. They had a flaming two-edged sword in their hands. The meaning of which turned every way is that the sword had two edges. Those who say that the flaming sword refers to the sun are incorrect.

At the east. Mi-kedem means at the east. Note, the story of the garden of Eden is to be interpreted literally. There is no doubt that it happened exactly as described in Scripture. Nevertheless, it also has a secret meaning. It alludes to the following: Intellect (the Garden of Eden) gave birth to desire (the tree of knowledge). Desire gave birth to man’s actions. It is via his actions that man can elevate himself, for the force that propels his desire is in front of him. The fig leaves prove this. Man’s actions are also called the testing ground, for by them man is tried. Intellect and desire are only potential. The one who understands the secrets of the tree of knowledge will understand the secret of the four rivers that divided into four parts (Bereshit 2:10). This is the secret of the Garden of Eden and the garments of skin. There is also an allusion in all of this to man’s potential immortality (the tree of life). The intelligent will understand that this is the ultimate purpose of man’s life on earth.

And the man. When Adam realized that he would not live forever he saw the need of perpetuating the human race. Chavah concurred and therefore exclaimed, upon giving birth to a child, I have gotten a man with the help of Hashem. Chavah used the Tetragrammaton, and not the term Elokim, because Hashem’s spirit now rested upon the earth via the human race even as it does on the heavenly bodies. The term good refers to creation as a whole. We thus read, And Elokim saw everything that He had made, and, behold, it was very good (Bereshit 1:31). Evil is found only in a part of creation.

And in process of time. That Kayin tilled the soil, he brought an offering to the place that he had set aside for his devotions. I disagree with those who say that he brought an offering to his father. There is support for the notion that Kayin did not bring his offering from the first of the fruits of the ground in Scripture’s stating that And Hevel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof.

And the Lord had respect. Va-yisha (and he had respect) follows the paradigm of va-yichar (and he was wroth) in And Kayin was very wroth (va-yichar). Va-yisha means, and he accepted. She’u in Look away (she’u) from me (Is. 22:4) is close in meaning to it. They brought offerings in keeping with the secret meaning of the sacrificial ritual. It is possible that a fire came down from heaven and consumed Hevel’s sacrifice but not Kayin’s.I believe that yamim (time) (v. 3) means a full year. Scripture similarly states, for a full year (yamim) shall he have the right of redemption (Vayikra 25:29). A year is called yamim (days) because it indicates that the full cycle of days, both long and short, has been completed. From year to year (mi-yamim yamimah) (Shemot 13:10) is similar. The meaning of shenatayim yamim (two full years) (Bereshit 41:1) is two complete years from day to day. Had Scripture read shenatayim (two years), then it would possibly not have meant two full years from day to day. Similarly ad chodesh yamim (but a whole month) (Bamidbar 11:20) refers to a complete cycle of the moon. I therefore maintain that when the prophet Daniel prophesied a thousand, two hundred and ninety days (yamim) (Daniel 12:11), he meant days and not years. I say this because the days (yamim) are enumerated.

Shall it not. Many commentators explain se’et (be lifted up) to mean thy sins will be forgiven. However, it appears to me that se’et means thy face will be lifted up. For it is previously written, and his countenance fell (v. 5). And his countenance fell indicates shame, as in how then should I hold up my face (esah panai) (Shmuel II 2:22). The meaning of our verse is: if you will do good, then you will lift up your face. Surely then shalt thou lift up thy face (tissa fanekha) without spot (Iyov 11:15) is similar.

Sin coucheth. Some say that chattat (sin) is used here in place of avon (iniquity). There are also those who explain this clause to mean that thy iniquity (sin) will couch over thy grave at the day of judgment. They further explain the pronominal suffix of teshukato (its desire) as referring to Hevel. Its meaning is, why are you wroth that I accepted Hevel’s sacrifice since he is obligated to obey thee (ve-elekha teshukato), and thou art a ruler over him? Others say that the pronominal suffix of teshukato (its desire) refers to the impulse (yetzer) even though this impulse (yetzer) is not mentioned in this verse. These commentators explain sin coucheth at the door as meaning that your sin lies in wait at the door of your house and is always with you. Others interpret door (petach) as referring to the door of the mouth, as in Keep the doors (pitche) of thy mouth (Michah 7:5). However, in my opinion the word chattat (sin) in sin coucheth at the door is in the construct, and it is the impulse of man’s heart that “coucheth” with him.
And unto thee is its desire. If you will it, then your impulse (yetzer) will obey you. Additionally, you have the power to rule over it.

And Kayin spoke. It appears to me that Kayin related to Hevel the full account of the rebuke with which Hashem had reproached him. Those born on a dark day ask, how did Kayin kill Hevel since no swords were yet in existence? This is a foolish question. He could have choked him or killed him with a stone or a piece of wood inasmuch as there were thousands of stones and chunks of wood around.
[Where.] Ay(where) means the same as ayeh. The word ayfo (where) is a combination of two words.

Crieth unto me. Crieth unto Me is not connected to voice of (kol). Similarly in Hark, my beloved (kol dodi)! behold, he cometh, (Cant. 2:8), he cometh is connected to my beloved, as I have pointed out in my commentary on Canticles. The meaning of our verse is: I have heard the cry of your brother’s blood that was poured out upon the ground. However, Onkelos interprets thy brother’s blood as referring to the potential descendants of Hevel.

And now cursed art thou from the ground. Kayin, a tiller of the soil, suffered a loss with regard to the ground. He sowed and planted but the earth no longer yielded fruits or harvest. Kayin was forced to wander far from the dwelling place of his father, Adam, who lived close to the Garden of Eden. He was never to find rest in one place but was constantly to be on the move.

[And a wanderer.] Some explain nad (wanderer) to mean a mourner, as in to bemoan (la-nud) him (Iyov 2:11). However, my opinion is that nad is a synonym for na (fugitive). Nedod (wander) in Lo, then would I wander (nedod) far off (Tehillim 55:8) is analogous.

[My punishment is greater than I can bear.] All the commentaries explain this to mean that Kayin confessed his sin. They say that the meaning of neso (bear) is forgiveness, as in forgiving iniquity (noseh avon) (Shemot 34:7). However, I disagree. In Hebrew reward is called ekev (heel), and the harsh punishment which comes as a result of iniquity is occasionally referred to as “sin.” Similarly we find, for the iniquity (avon) of the Emori is not yet full (Bereshit 15:16); there shall no punishment (avon) happen to thee (Shmuel I 28:10); For the iniquity (avon) of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sedom (Eichah 4:6). The meaning of our verse thus is: my punishment (avon) is greater than I can bear (mi-neso). The next verse substantiates this interpretation.
Patzetah (v.11) is to be rendered opened. Yiftzeh (doth open) in But Iyov doth open (yiftzeh) his mouth in vanity (Iyov 35:16) is similar.
[And from thy face shall I be hid.] All the world is full of Hashem’s glory. Nevertheless, there are places more receptive to Hashem’s power, and His might is seen there.

Sevenfold. Until seven generations, for shivatayim (sevenfold) does not mean fourteen, nor does it mean three hundred and forty-three. Proof that shivatayim means sevenfold is that the prophet states, And the light of the sun shall be sevenfold (shivatayim) and then explains his words, viz., as the light of the seven days (Is. 30:26).

[Vengeance shall be taken on him.] The meaning of yukkam (vengeance shall be taken on him) is that vengeance shall be exacted from him. He shall not be punished (yukkam) (Shemot 21:21) is similar. The meaning of our verse is that Hashem held back his anger and waited seven generations before punishing Kayin. Don’t ask, how could Kayin’s life span extend for seven generations? Behold, his brother Shet lived many years with Noach. It is also possible that Kayin’s descendants are called Kayin after their patriarch in the same way that Yehudim are called Yisrael. Some say that the sign Hashem set for Kayin was a horn. Others say Hashem removed fear from Kayin’s heart and gave him courage to face the world. It appears to me that Hashem gave Kayin a sign that no harm would befall him. Kayin finally believed Hashem because of the sign. Scripture, however, does not tell us what the sign was.
In the land of Nod. The land of Nod is so called because it was in that land that Kayin was a wanderer and a fugitive.
On the east side of Eden. East of Eden and north of the garden.
[Chanoch.] The city was called after Chanoch, the son of Kayin. Similarly the city of Shomron was called after Shamer (Melachim I 16:24) and Mitzrayim (mitzraim) was named for Mitzraim, son of Cham.
Lemech was the seventh generation from Adam and the sixth from Kayin.

[Adah and…zillah.] Do not pay attention to Saadiah Gaon’s interpretation of Biblical names. Even if we knew Hebrew perfectly, how would we be able to ascertain the events which they commemorate? If the Bible did not state why Moshe was named Moshe, or Issaschar, Issaschar, would we be able to surmise the meaning of these names?

[The father of such as dwell in tents.] The meaning of avi (father of) is first. The same is true of the word av (father) and the word (aviv) (spring). When the word for father is in the construct it always has a yod suffixed to it. The same is true with the word for brother.
The harp and pipe. Harp and pipe (kinnor ve-ugav) are types of musical instruments. The ability to play these instruments requires great wisdom.
The forger. Lotesh (the forger) means the sharpener. Li-litosh in to sharpen (li-litosh) every man his plowshare (Shmuel I 13:20) is similar.

[And Lemech said…] Note, this should have appeared earlier. I have already noted two similar examples of this in my earlier comments. Three additional examples are: that the man took a golden ring (Bereshit 24:22); And the Lord said unto Moshe, say unto the children of Yisrael: Ye are a stiff-necked people (Shemot 33:5); and And I besought the Lord at that time (Devarim 3:23). As to our verse, it is to be interpreted as our sages did. The rabbis tell us that Adah and Tzilah were afraid to bear children because they feared that their offspring, who were the seventh generation from Kayin, would die or be killed as punishment for Kayin’s sin. Therefore Lemech said to them, “I am in truth the seventh generation and if a man would wound me or a child bruise me, then I would kill them.” I have slain is used in place of I will slay. Similar examples are: I will give (natati) the price of the field (Bereshit 23:13), and which I took out of the hand of the Emori (Bereshit 48:22). There are many similar instances.

Lemech said to his wives, If Kayin shall be avenged sevenfold, Truly Lemech seventy and sevenfold because Kayin deliberately murdered and he, Lemech, did not. In other words, Lemech told his wives that the decree upon Kayin was annulled. However, the fact of the matter is that Lemech’s children and all his seed perished in the deluge. Thus Kayin’s name was wiped out because he murdered his brother.
[Instead of Hevel.] That is, in place of Hevel.

[Began to call.] Huchal (began) belongs to those verbs whose second and third root letters are identical. If the chet were not a guttural, it would receive a dagesh. Huchal comes from the same root as techil’ah (first). The meaning of the clause then began (huchal) men to call upon the name of Hashem is: then men first started praying. If huchal were derived from chillul (profane), then the name of Hashem would follow profane.
This is the book of the generations of Adam. The children and grandchildren that he begot. Adam and only Adam had no human parents, for he was created by Elokim in the likeness of Elokim.

Scripture notes that Adam begat a son in his own likeness, after his image (v. 3) to teach us that Hashem implanted in Adam the power to reproduce his Hashem like image so that his work would be like that of Hashem. Scripture does not say the same with regard to Kayin and Hevel, nor does it state how long Kayin lived or how old Kayin was when he begot his son Chanoch. It omits the above clause because the former was murdered and the latter’s descendants perished in the deluge. The Torah tells the story of the murderer Kayin to stress Hashem’s righteousness. Hashem was long-suffering with Kayin but he ultimately punished him. This is in keeping with and that (Hashem) will by no means clear the guilty (Shemot 34:7).

Chanoch. Son of Yered. Scripture says about Chanoch, And Chanoch walked with Elokim. The meaning of this is the same as the meaning of After Hashem your Elokim shall ye walk (Devarim 13:5). The same thing is stated concerning Noach, namely, Noach walked with Elokim (Bereshit 6:9). Others say that Noach walked with Elokim means he trained himself to walk with Elokim.

And he was not; for Elokim took him. That is, he died. So, too, take, I beseech Thee, my life from me (Yonah 4:3). Scripture similarly states, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes (Yechezkel 24:16) and then explains its meaning, namely, his wife died (Yechezkel 24:18). The Bible does not state with regard to Chanoch’s being taken that Chanoch died, nor is there any reference to a plague causing his death. The meaning of took him in our verse is similar to take me in the psalm of Asaf, And afterward take me with glory (Tehillim 73:24), and He shall take me, in the psalm of the sons of Korach, But Elokim will redeem my soul from the power of the netherworld; For He shall take me (Tehillim 49:16). The intelligent will understand this.

[This same shall comfort us.] Lemech was informed by Adam, who was a prophet, that through his newborn child the land would live. Or perhaps they learned the aforementioned through astrology. And so it was, for it was through Noach that the world was preserved. Furthermore, Noach was, as the Bible explicitly states, an expert in agriculture (Bereshit 9:20). It is also possible that he got this name after his agricultural successes. We find the same with Yeruba'al. Noach (rest) is the opposite of toil (etzavon). The meaning of our verse is, this one will comfort us and we will rest (nanu’ach) from the toil of our hands. Moreover, comfort is a relaxation of the heart’s pain. The Hebrews are more concerned with the idea expressed by a word than with its etymology. Proof of the above is the fact that Yeruba'al is referred to as Yerubeshet. Those who ask whom Kayin and Shet married raise a worthless question. Scripture tells us that Adam begot sons and daughters. The same is true of all of them.
[Began.] Hechel (began) is a hifil. It is a denominative of techillah (beginning).
To multiply. La-rov (to multiply) is an infinitive.

The sons of Elokim. The term bene Elokim (the sons of god) refers to the sons of the judges who dispensed Elokim’s (Elokim) justice. Others say that Elokim refers to Elokim Himself and the sons of Elokim are holy ones (saints) living on earth. They are called sons of Elokim in the sense of Ye are the children of the Lord your Elokim (Devarim 14:1). Others say that the sons of Elokim refers to the children of Shet and that the daughters of man refers to women of Kayin’s family. However, it appears to me that the sons of Elokim refers to those who know the will of the most High. These men chose women who matched them astrologically and physically. Hence they produced mighty men. It is possible that they took women even against their will.

My spirit shall not abide. Some say that yadon (shall abide) is like the word nedanah (sheath thereof), as in and he put up his sword back into the sheath thereof (nedanah) (Divrei Hayamim I 21:27), for the body serves as a sheath for the spirit. Proof of this is found in my spirit was pained in the midst of my body (nidneh) (Daniel 7:15). Nevertheless, nadan and yadon come from different roots. We find the same with the words nasah (lifted) and si’o (his excellency). We read, Though his excellency (si’o) mount up to the heavens (Iyov 20:6). The root of si’o is sin, vav, alef. Nevertheless, a word derived from nasah (lifted) (whose root is nun, sin, alef) would have a similar meaning. There are many examples of this. Others say that yadon follows the paradigm of ve-yashov (returneth), as in And the dust returneth (ve-yashov) to the earth as it was (Kohelet 12:7). They say that yadon comes from the same root as din (to judge) because the spirit judges the body.
