Note: Each one of the seven nations that dwelled in Kenaan were Kenaani. They descended from Kenaan, who fathered eleven sons. Elsewhere Scripture lists six Kenaani nations by their specific names and includes the remainder under the term Kenaani. In our chapter Scripture lists ten of them. At other times Scripture includes them all in the term Kenaani without enumerating them. Scripture similarly states, Yehudah and Yisrael were many (Melachim I 4:20) even though the term Yisrael includes Yehudah.

It may be that I shall be builded up. Ibbaneh (I shall be builded up) comes from the same root as ben (son). It is possible that the word for son (ben) comes from the root bet, nun, heh (to build), with the heh dropped because, metaphorically speaking, the father serves as the foundation and the son as the building. Chai (life) in the third person perfect and in the adjectival form is similar.
And Avram hearkened. Avraham said yes to her.

After Avram had dwelt ten years in the land of Kenaan. Our sages, of blessed memory, transmitted a law that a man shall not remain married more that ten years to a woman who has not borne him a child. They used this verse as sort of a support for this law. It is a good support.
Was despised. The tzere in va-tekal (was despised) is in place of the dagesh which should be placed in the kof to make up for one of the missing root letters. Va-tekal is a nifal.
Found her. Va-yimtza’ah (found her) is irregular. It should have been vocalized like va-yisna’eha (and he hateth her) (Devarim 22:16).

Whence. Ay (whence) means where. Ay (where) in Where is (ay) Hevel thy brother (Bereshit 4:9) is similar. Mi-zeh (from this) is short for mi-zeh makom (from this place). The meaning of ai mi-zeh vat is: where is the place thou camest from?

I flee. The resh of borachat (I flee) is vocalized with a pattach because it is followed by a guttural. These are similar: borachat (fleeth) in The whole city fleeth (borachat) (Yirmiyahu 4:29); porachat (budding) in and as it was budding (khe-forachat) (Bereshit 40:10); rachat (shovel) in with the shovel (va-rachat) and with the fan (Is. 30:24); and yoda’at (known) in that hath known man (yoda’at ish) (Bamidbar 31:17). The reason the middle letter of the root of the above words is vocalized with a pattach is that it precedes gutturals. They are: alef, chet, heh, ayin. This is the rule. There is no exception.
Behold thou. Hinnakh (behold thou) is the form used when a female is being addressed, because it is a preposition. It is like the word im (with); it follows the paradigm of immakh (with you).
Yishmael. The alef of Yishmael is not pronounced to simplify enunciation.

A wild ass of a man. He will be free among men. Compare, Who hath sent out the wild ass free (Iyov 39:5). The meaning of our clause is that no stranger will rule over him. Others say that we should render perah adam (a wild ass of a man) by a wild ass and a man. It is like The sun and moon stand still in their habitation ((Chavakuk 3:11). The meaning of our verse is: because he will be a wild ass his hand shall be against every man, but because he is a man every man’s hand (shall be) against him. In my opinion its interpretation is: he will be as a wild ass among men; i.e., he will overcome men. However, ultimately every man’s hand (shall be) against him. This is clearly stated in the book of Daniel, for the fourth beast described therein refers to the kingdom of Yishmael.

And he shall dwell in the face of all his brethren. The latter being the children of Keturah. It is similarly written, over against all his brethren did he settle (Bereshit 25:18). Also, the Midyanim are of the children of Keturah. However, they are referred to as Yishmeelim in the Pentateuch and in the Book of Shoftim.

A God of seeing. Ro’ i (seeing) follows the paradigm of oni (affliction). Compare, I am the man that hath seen affliction (oni) (Eichah 3:1). The meaning of a God of seeing is a God who appears in visions.

Have I even here. The commentaries translate halom as now. However, its correct meaning is here. Halom (hither) in Is there yet a man come hither (halom) (Shmuel I 10:22) is similar. The meaning ha-gam halom ra’iti achare ro’ i (have I even here seen Him that seeth me) is: have I even here seen an angel of Hashem after Hashem saw my affliction, because Hashem constantly seeth me (ro’i).

Beer-lahai. Be'er lahai means the well of him who will be alive next year. Compare, ko le-chai (so to life next year) (Shmuel I 25:6). The well was so called because the Yishmeelim held annual festivities at this well. It is still in existence and is called the well of zamum.

Hashem Almighty. Shaddai is an adjective meaning mighty. Shaddai in like a mighty voice (ke-kol shaddai) (Yechezkel 1:24) is similar. Also, Shaddai in And mighty will be thy silver (shaddai betzarekha) (Iyov 22:25) is similar because the word betzarekha (thy silver) has the same meaning as the word betzer (silver) in And lay thy treasure (or silver) (betzer) in the dust (Iyov 22:24). The word Shaddai follows the paradigm of davvai (faint), in And my heart is faint (davvai) (Eichah 1:22). Many derive Shaddai from the same root as shoded (overpowering), meaning, He is victorious and overpowering. The reason Hashem used this name at this time was to impress upon Avraham the fear of Hashem so that he would circumcise himself. The correct interpretation of the divine names is as follows: Shaddai is an adjective describing Hashem’s power over creation. The Tetragrammaton, Hashem’s revered and awesome name, stands in contrast to it. The world exists by virtue of these two names. Whoever understands the secret of Hashem’s name will accept my interpretation.
And be thou whole-hearted. Do not question the reason for circumcision.

Avraham. The new name with the addition of the resh means the mighty one of a multitude of nations. This is so because the new name did not come to diminish a letter from Avraham’s original name but to add one.

Sarah, unlike Sarai, is a general adjective. Blessed be Hashem before whom all actions are weighed. He commanded Avraham to circumcise himself before Sarah became pregnant so that his seed would be holy.

[Every male among you shall be circumcised.] Himmol (shall be circumcised) is to be read as if it had a lamed prefixed to it. It is an infinitive. It belongs to the verbs having a vav as the middle letter of their root. It is like va-yamal in and circumcised (va-yamal) the flesh of their foreskin (v. 23). It follows the paradigm of le-hikkon (to be prepared).

And ye shall be circumcised. U-nemaltem (and ye shall be circumcised) is similar to u-shemartem (and ye shall keep). The nun of u-nemaltem is a root letter. Yadon (shall be sheathed) in My spirit shall not be sheathed (yadon) (Bereshit 6:3) and nidneh (sheath) (Daniel 7:15) are similar.

Shall be circumcised among you. Yimmol (shall be circumcised) is a nifal, as are himmol yimmol (must needs be circumcised) (v. 13). Why does Scripture state twice, He that is born in thy house…must needs be circumcised? This is the answer: Scripture first states that in the future all males, those of thy seed and also those born in the house or bought with money, shall be circumcised on the eighth day. It then states, “ Avraham immediately circumcise all males born in thy house and he that is bought with thy money although they are adults.”

And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised. Yimmol (is circumcised) is a kal. It is like yiddor (voweth) in When a man voweth (yiddor) a vow (Bamidbar 30:3). It comes from the same root as u-nemaltem (and ye shall be circumcised) in and ye shall be circumcised (u-nemaltem) in the flesh of your foreskin (v. 11). The meaning of the verse is, a male who reaches the age when he is obligated to observe the commandments of the Torah and does not circumcise himself is subject to the penalty of karet (being cut off). The verse refers to an adult because while a person is yet a child, the obligation to circumcise him falls upon his father. However, should his father fail to do so, then upon reaching maturity he must circumcise himself. Karet (being cut off) is a penalty inflicted by God. Those who err hold that a child that dies uncircumcised does not have a share in the world to come. However, the meaning of the word nefesh is not as they think, a soul, but a person; it means a body containing a soul. Similarly, If anyone (nefesh) shall sin (Vayikra 4:2). Some say that karet refers to death before the age of fifty-two. Others say it means the eradication of one’s name via the death of one’s children. Therefore Scripture states, that soul shall be cut off from his people, for a person who leaves children is considered to live on even after his death, and his name is not cut off.

And moreover I will give thee. Natati (I will give thee) in our verse is like natati in I will give (natati) the price of the field (Bereshit 23:13). Observe, although both are perfects, they are to be rendered as imperfects.

Shall a child be born unto him that is a hundred years old. Avraham was amazed at being told that he would have a son because the sperm of an old man is cold and therefore aged men are infertile. However, he was even more amazed that Sarah, a woman whose menstrual cycle had ceased, would bear a child, since the embryo is made and constructed from the woman’s menstrual blood. If you will reflect you will conclude that Sarah’s conceiving was a greater wonder than Avraham’s begetting a child. For we find instances of men over ninety begetting children in later generations, and the life span of people in Avraham’s time was much longer than in later times. As soon as the angel left, Avraham immediately circumcised Yishmael and all those born in his house and those bought with money.

In the selfsame day. Avraham did not hesitate to carry out the commandment of circumcision. Behold, Avraham’s household consisted of three hundred eighteen males born in his house aside from those bought with his money. After circumcising them, Avraham circumcised himself on that very day. Now Yishmael his son plus all those born in his house and bought with his money were voluntarily circumcised with him (Avraham) (v. 27). For the meaning of “with him” (v. 27) is that Avraham did not have to force his household to comply with Hashem’s commandment. They all voluntarily hurried to do and fulfill Hashem’s will.
Were circumcised with him. Nimmolu (were circumcised) is a nifal. Its root is nun, mem, lamed. Ve-nishlo’ach (were sent) in And letters were sent (ve-nishlo’ach sefarim) (Est. 3:13) is similar.

And Hashem appeared. Behold, a few say that Hashem is three men: He is one and He is three and they are inseparable. They forget that Scripture expressly states, And the two angels came to Sedom at even. However, the commentaries tell us that Hashem first appeared to Avraham in a vision after which Avraham lifted up his eyes and saw three angels. One came to bring happy tidings to Sarah and the other two went on to Sedom, one to destroy it and one to save Lot.
The meaning of And they did eat (v. 8) is that the bread was consumed. Eaten, in our verse, has the same meaning as the identical word in whereto the fire hath eaten (consumed) (Vayikra 6:3).

[Forasmuch as ye are come.] Ki al ken avartem (forasmuch as ye are come) means the same as ho’il va-avartem (since you are come) in Rabbinic Hebrew. It is like forasmuch as (ki al ken) as they are come under the shadow of my roof (Bereshit 19:8).
So do, as thou hast said. They responded politely and said to him that a morsel of bread would suffice.
Knead it. Lushi (knead it) is like va-talash (and kneaded it) (Shmuel I 28:24).

When the season cometh round. Ka-et (when the season) means next year, at this time, and chayyah (cometh round), that Sarah will then be alive. It is like ko le-chai (so to life next year) (Shmuel I 25:6).

Which was behind him. The angel who spoke to Avraham was behind the tent. Avraham sat in the tent door and consequently could not see Sarah. Others say that the door of Sarah’s tent was behind the tent of Avraham.
And well stricken in age. They lived many days.
Shall I have. Hayetah li means shall I have.

Pleasure. The word ednah means pleasure and enjoyment. Va-yitaddenu (and luxuriated) in and luxuriated (va-yitaddenu) in Thy great goodness (Nechemyah 9:25) is similar. The meaning of our verse is: How can the enjoyment and pleasure of youth be renewed in me, seeing that I have waxed old and aged and my husband, too, is old.
[Within herself.] In her mind. Hashem revealed Sarah’s inner thoughts to the angel.
Whom am old. This explains After I am waxed old. The angel spoke the truth.

The mem of umnam (of a surety) is not a root letter. It is like the mem of shilshom (the day before yesterday) (Bereshit 31:5). Other commentators maintain that Avraham’s three guests were prophets. If one should argue, why would Hashem send a message via a prophet to Avraham who himself was a prophet, since it is only when one prophet is greater than the other, as in the case of Moshe who was sent with a prophesy to Aharon, that Hashem transmits his intentions to a prophet through another prophet, then they would answer that the three prophets came not to Avraham but to Sarah. Indeed, Scripture explicitly states, And they said unto him: Where is Sarah thy wife (v. 9). After one of the prophets delivered the message to Sarah, the other two went on to Sedom. Also, do not be troubled by the clause for we will destroy this place (Gen.19:13), as we find a similar expression with regard to Moshe and Aharon: And Moshe and Aharon did all these wonders before Paroh (Shemot 11:10). In reality Hashem did the wonders and they were attributed to Moshe and Aharon because they were the agents by which the miracles were performed. Now according to this interpretation, and they did eat (v. 8) is to be taken literally. Similarly, according to this interpretation, the term Adonai (Hashem) in My lord, (Adonai) if now I have found favor in thy sight (v. 3) does not refer to the Deity, but means my lords. Hence there is a pattach beneath the nun, and it is not vocalized with a kamatz as would be the case if it referred to Hashem. However, in those copies of the Pentateuch where Adonai is vocalized with a kamatz the term must be interpreted as: O prophet of Hashem. Also (according to the aforementioned interpretation), the reason Avraham said, if now I have found favor in thy sight (v. 3) is that he first addressed the most important of the three and then the other two. Those who maintain that the three who visited Avraham were prophets point out that the prophet Chaggai is referred to in Scripture as an angel. Others say that Adonai means Hashem and that Avraham respectfully requested that Hashem wait until he had attended his guests. There are still others who say that the verses are not in order of their occurrence. According to this interpretation, And he lifted up (v. 2) is to be interpreted: and he had already lifted up his eyes and looked and done so and so. After this, Hashem appeared to him and said, Shall I hide from Avraham that which I am doing, etc. (v. 17), and Verily the cry of Sedom and Amorah is great, etc. (v. 20). But Avraham stood yet before Hashem (v. 22) when the two angels who left for Sedom arrived there. In any case, And Hashem said: Shall I hide from Avraham that which I am doing, etc., relates either to what Hashem directly revealed to Avraham or to what He told the angels to relate to Avraham. However, all opinions agree that And Hashem said: Verily the cry of Sedom and Amorah is great, and verily their sin is exceedingly grievous, etc. (v. 20 and 21), definitely records Hashem’s words to Avraham. Upon hearing this, Avraham drew near and said, Wilt thou indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked, etc. (v. 23-32).And the men turned from thence, and went toward Sedom; but Avraham stood yet before Hashem, (v. 22) is a parenthetical statement noting that at the very moment that the men came to Sedom, Hashem told Avraham, Verily, the cry of Sedom and Amorah is great. This is similar: As they were going down at the end of the city, Shmuel said to Shaul: ‘Bid the servant pass on before us - and he passed on - but stand thou still at this time, that I may cause thee to hear the word of Hashem’ (Shmuel I 9:27). There is no need to assume that the scribes changed the original reading of our verse from but Hashem stood yet before Avraham to but Avraham stood yet before Hashem. Indeed, the verse And Avraham got up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before Hashem (Bereshit 19:27) proves that there was no scribal emendation. I will allude to my own beliefs with regard to the appearance of the angels in my commentary on the first Torah portion of Exodus.

[Is anything too hard for Hashem?] Ha-yippale (is it too hard) means is it hidden. Fele (hidden things) in oseh fele (doing hidden things) (Shemot 15:11) is similar. Others say the meaning of ha-yippale me-adonai davar is: it is not a wonder in Hashem’s eyes to do such a thing. However, if this were so, then a mem would not be prefixed to Hashem’s name.

Shall be blessed in him. Ve-nivrikhu (shall be blessed) is a nifal. It means that they shall be blessed because of Avraham. However, ve-hitbarekhu (Bereshit 22:18) has a different meaning. It means: they shall bless themselves in him.
[Verily the cry of Sedom.] Either the cry of its blasphemy or the cry of those victimized by its violence.
And, verily, their sin is exceedingly grievous. And the earth cannot bear it.
[I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it.] Some say this verse is to be interpreted as follows: If they have done so then I will destroy them (kalah).

And if not, I will know. Eda’ah means I will have pity upon them. They similarly interpret va-yeda Elokim (and Elokim took cognizance of them) (Shemot 2:25). However, I believe that this verse is to be explained as follows: I will go down and see if all of them (kalah) have done this evil. For in truth, Elokim who is All knows the individual in a general rather than in a detailed manner. Proof that this interpretation is correct, although it is a great mystery, is Avraham’s plea, Wilt thou indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked (v. 23). The heh of ha’af (wilt) is vocalized with a pattach even though it is an interrogative heh, because it is followed by an alef, which is a guttural, and it is the rule in Hebrew to elongate the vowel before gutturals.

That wilt sweep away. Tispeh (thou wilt sweep away) is a transitive verb. It means is thou wilt destroy (or finish). Aspeh (finish) in I will finish (aspeh) evils upon them (Devarim 32:23) is similar. Both words (tispeh and aspeh) mean the same thing even though they belong to different conjugations.
And not forgive the place. Tissa means forgive. Compare, nose (forgiving) in forgiving iniquity (nose avon) (Shemot 34:7).
[The place.] Sedom. For it was on account of Sedom that Avraham approached God in prayer. He did so to save Lot.
That be far. Chalilah (that be far) means it is not possible. Others say that chalilah (that be far) is to be connected to the word chalul, which means empty.

That so the righteous should be as the wicked. When two cafs are prefixed to two words following each other we are dealing with an abridged statement. Hence our verse should be understood as follows: that so the righteous should be as the wicked and the wicked be so as the righteous. Similarly, for thou art even as Paroh (Bereshit 44:18); my people as thy people (Melachim I 22:4); and The darkness is even as the light (Tehillim 139:12). The thrust of Avraham’s appeal is: How is it possible for the Judge of all the earth to act unjustly?

[Within the city.] That is, who publicly revere My name. Run ye to and fro through the streets of Yerushalayim, And see now, and know, And seek in the broad places thereof, If ye can find a man, If there be any that doeth justly, and seeketh truth; And I will pardon her (Yirmiyahu 5:1) is similar.

[I have taken upon me.] Ho’alti (I have taken upon me) does not mean I began; it means I wanted. Ho’il Moshe (took Moshe upon him) (Devarim 1:5) is similar. The caf of anokhi (I) is superfluous. On the other hand, it is possible that there are two different words for I in Hebrew.
[Who am but dust and ashes.] For dust I was and ashes I will be. Avraham was speaking only about the body’s foundation, i.e., its skeletal frame.
Peradventure there shall lack five. Perhaps a tenth of the number will be lacking.

[Wilt thou destroy all the city for lack of five.] Will you destroy the city because of the five who are missing from the fifty? Avraham then repeated his request and said, “Will you destroy the city if a ninth are missing from the number (forty-five) concerning which you stated that if there be found there that many righteous men I will not destroy them.”

[I will not do it for the forty’s sake.] I will not do it means I will not bring destruction. And so as not to prolong his prayers Avraham combined the two previous subtractions. Thus Avraham asked if one quarter of the forty was missing would God destroy the city. He then asked if a third of the thirty were missing, would God destroy it. He concluded by asking if God would destroy the city if half of the twenty righteous men were missing. Some say that Avraham did not ask God to spare for less than ten people because there were five cities and thus less than two righteous per city. However, they are mistaken, for Scripture expressly tells us that Avraham spoke only of Sedom. Now even though our sages, of blessed memory, transmitted as mere tradition the law that there can be no public prayer when fewer than ten men are present, this verse may be taken as a support of our faith in the law which they passed on to us.

And Avraham returned unto his place. To Chevron. This vision took place at the spot where Avraham went to accompany the angels on their way. From this spot Avraham looked out toward Sedom. And he (Avraham) looked out toward Sedom and Amorah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and lo, the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace (Bereshit 19:28) took place after sunrise. This is so even though the preceding verse opens with And Avraham got up early in the morning. This is so because Sedom was not destroyed at night. The latter is clearly noted in Scripture.
[At even.] The term ba-erev (at even) will be explained in the chapter dealing with the Passover observed by Bnei Yisrael in Mitzrayim.
And he fell down on his face to the earth. Until his nose touched the earth. Appayim (his face) refers to the nostrils which protrude from the face.

Behold now, my lords. Adonai is to be rendered my lords. It does not refer to God. When the word sur (turn aside) is followed by a mem it means to turn away from. When it is followed by the word el (to) it means turn from your place and come here, or turn from your place and go to a designated place. Compare, surah elai (turn in to me) (Jud. 4:18).

And they said: “nay.” Unless you urge us to do so. The word va-yiftzar (and he urged) indicates the use of many conciliatory words. Haftzar (stubbornness) in And stubbornness (haftzar) is as idolatry and teraphim (Shmuel I 15:23) is similar.
Compassed. Nasabbu (compassed) is a nifal.
All the people from every quarter. Those who did not live in the vicinity of Lot’s house.
That we may know them. A euphemism for sexual intercourse.
To the door. Ha-petchah means to the door. The tav of the word delet (door) is the sign of the feminine. The word delet is also found spelled without the tav.
Known man. The third person plural perfect is the same in both the masculine and feminine when not written with a vav conversive which is vocalized with a pattach.

These. Ha-el (these) means the same as ha-eleh. Saadiah Gaon claims that Scripture used the term ha-el because one of the three angels was missing. However, his comment is far-fetched, for the Aramaic translation of the Pentateuch renders both ha-el and ha-eleh by the same word.
With blindness. Sanverim (blindness) has a quadriliteral root. This term is also found in the account of Elisha (Melachim II 6:18). It refers to physical and intellectual blindness.
Hast thou here any besides? Son-in-law. If you have a son-in-law here.

And thy sons, and thy daughters. Or sons-in-law who are considered as your sons and daughters. We have here a refutation of the opinion that maintains that one of the two angels was sent to save Lot. For behold, both angels spoke to Lot. Furthermore, they said to him, for we will destroy this place (v. 13). Also, Lot later said to the angel, behold now, thy servant hath found grace in thy sight, and thou hast magnified thy mercy, which thou hast shown unto me in saving my life, etc. (v. 19). Now that very angel replied to Lot, Hasten thou, escape thither, for I cannot do anything till thou be come thither (v. 22).
Who married his daughters. Lot had two other daughters who perished in Sedom. This is clear from Scripture’s statement: Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters that are here (v. 15).

And when the morning arose. Rabbi Yonah, the Spanish grammarian, said that it is ungrammatical to say u-khemo alah ha-shachar (and when arose the morning). However, Rabbi Yonah seems to have forgotten the verse ve-ravu kemo ravu (and they shall increase as they have increased) (Zecharyah 10:8).
Then the angels hastened. Va-ya’itzu (hastened) means they pressured. Compare, And the taskmasters were urgent (atzim), saying (Shemot 5:13).

[But he lingered.] I am amazed by Ben Efraim’s commentary. He claims that va-yitmahmah (but he lingered) is derived from the same root as mah (what). However, he seems to have forgotten that both hehs of va-yitmahmah are pointed. In reality va-yitmahmah means lingered. It comes from a triliteral root with the first letter written twice.
And the men laid hold upon his hand. The verse notes that Lot was overcome with fear and had no strength to flee on his own.

[When they had brought them forth.] Ke-hotzi’am (when they had brought) is an infinitive. Ke-hotzi’am should not be confused with le-hotzi’am (to bring them out), in to bring them out (le-hotzi’am) of the land of Mitzrayim (Yirmiyahu 31:32), for in our verse the mem suffix stands for the subject, i.e., the angels. The object of the sentence, Lot and his family, are indicated by the word otam (them).
Look not behind thee. Neither you nor any that belong to you. Thou shalt not eat of it (Bereshit 2:17) is similar.

Oh, not so my Lord. Adonai (my lord) does not refer to God. It is vocalized with a kamatz only because it comes at the end of the verse. Rabbi Shmuel Ha-Nagid the Spaniard, of blessed memory, said that al (not so) in al na (Oh, not so) is derived from the same root as ho’il (wanted, was willing). However, I believe that al means no. The meaning of our verse is as follows: When the angels told Lot, escape to the mountain, Lot replied, “Oh, not so my lords.”

He then turned to one of the angels and said, behold now, thy servant hath found grace in thy sight, etc. (v. 19). He did so because he considered this angel to be the more important of the two. The truth is that even among angels there are superiors who lord it over other angels. The tav of the root of mavet (death) is dropped in the word va-matti (and I die). The reason for this is that in the first person perfect a tav and a yod are added to the root. When the tav of the stem and the tav of the suffix come together, the tav of the root is lost in the pronunciation. The word ve-kharatta (and cut down) in them thou mayest destroy and cut down (ve-kharatta) (Devarim 20:20) is similar.

A little one. The meaning of mitzar (a little one) is small. It comes from the same root as tza’ir (young, little). It is an adjective. Even so, it is written without a heh at its end. Compare, shegal (consort).
From Hashem. This is a poetic way of saying from Himself. We similarly find Scripture repeating the term the children of Yisrael five times in one verse (Bamidbar 8:19).
And that which grew upon the ground. The trees growing there were consumed.
From behind him. From behind Lot.

A pillar. Nitziv (pillar) means the same as matzevah. Her bones were burned by brimstone and she was encrusted in salt, for it is written, brimstone, and salt…like the overthrow of Sedom and Amorah, Admah and Tzevoyim (Devarim 29:22). This verse also shows that Tzoar was not destroyed. The latter is also borne out by the words of the angel.
As the smoke of. Ke-kitor means as the smoke of. Kitor is derived from the same root as ketoret (incense).
A furnace. A place where fire is continually burning.

When he overthrew the cities in which lot dwelt. In one of which Lot had been living. Each of these is similar: Then died Yiftach the Giladi, and was buried in the cities of Gilad (Jud. 12:7); Even upon a colt the foal of she-asses (Zecharyah 9:9); and And if a man take with his wife also her mother, it is wickedness: they shall be burnt with fire, both he and they (Vayikra 20:14).

And the first-born said. Lot possibly had a wife who predeceased the wife who turned into a pillar of salt. Lot’s daughters thought that the world was destroyed by fire and brimstone in the same manner that it had previously been destroyed by the flood.

When she lay down. Be-shichvah (when she lay down) is an infinitive even though it is vocalized with a chirik beneath the shin. Be-shivri in When I break (be-shivri) your staff of bread (Vayikra 26:26) is similar.
Moav. Moav is the same as me-av and means from a father.
[Unto this day.] No other people were intermingled with them. Unto this day may also signify that the incestuous origin of the Moavim is known to this day.
Of Sarah his wife. The word el in el Sarah (of Sarah) should be rendered al (of, concerning). El in For (el) this child I prayed (Shmuel I 1:27) is similar.

The angel appeared to Avimelech in a dream because of God’s regard for Avraham’s honor. Scripture tells us that both Avimelech and Paroh took Sarah; nevertheless, God brought upon Paroh and his house great plagues, while the plagues brought on Avimelech and his house were of a lesser nature. The reason for this is that Avimelech was more righteous than Paroh.

[Lord, wilt thou slay even a righteous nation?] The term nation includes Avimelech, his household and his kingdom. That this is so can be seen from Scripture. Pay no attention to the dreamer who changes the terms used in Scripture. The latter explains goy (nation) to mean ish (a person). I will elaborate a bit upon this in my comments on the verse to sell her unto a foreign people he shall have no power (Shemot 21:8).
To touch. Li-nego’a (to touch) means the same as la-ga’at. The same is true with li-neto’a (to plant) and la-ta’at. All of the above are infinitives.
What hast thou done unto us? Meh (what) is vocalized with a segol because it precedes a guttural. This is the rule in Hebrew grammar.

And moreover she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father. Some say that this verse is to be understood in the same way as O Elokim of my father Avraham (Bereshit 32:10). However, I believe that Avraham put Avimelech off with a timely excuse. When we come to the verse I am Esav thy first-born (Bereshit 27:19), I will offer other examples of the same.

When Elokim caused me to wander. The word Elokim is to be rendered as Elokim. The meaning of hitu oti Elokim (Elokim caused me to wander) is that Elokim made Avraham journey from place to place without Avraham knowing where he would go next. To’eh (wandering) in and, behold he was wandering (to’eh) in the field (Bereshit 37:15) is similar. Hitu (caused me to wander) in our verse is not to be translated as caused me to err. We find the Bible using the word to’eh in the sense of erring in O Hashem, why does Thou make us to err (tatenu) from thy ways (Is. 63:17).
Say of me. Imri li is to be rendered: say of me. And Paroh will say of the children of (le-vene) Yisrael (Shemot 14:3) is similar.

Behold, it is for thee a covering of the eyes. Some say that this alludes to the dimming of her son’s (Yitzchak’s) eyes. However, the latter is a Midrashic interpretation. I believe that the phrase kesut enayim (a covering of the eyes) is to be read as if written twice. It is similar to the word not (al) in O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger, and chasten me in Thy wrath (Tehillim 38:2). There are many other such examples in Scripture. Our verse is to be interpreted as follows: Behold, he, viz., Avraham thy husband, is for thee as a covering of the eyes, i.e., no one will dare lift up his eyes to thee. He is similarly a covering of the eyes to all that are with thee, namely, the handmaidens who are married to his servants. Furthermore, the vav of ve-nokhachat (thou are righted) is rather like the Arabic fa. There are thousands of similar vavs in Scripture, an example being On the third day Avraham lifted up (va-yissa) his eyes (Bereshit 22:4). Ve-nokhachat (thou are righted) is a comment by Moshe, who added that Sarah did not ever again claim that Avraham was her brother. The meaning of ve-et kol (and before all men) is: after all this; i.e., after all this Sarah was chastened. Others explain that behold, it is for thee refers to money which Avimelech gave for the purchase of a garment, and it is the word natati (I have given) that is to be read as if written twice. The verse is to be interpreted as follows: Behold, I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver to buy thee a covering (kesut), meaning a garment, that is appealing to the eye (enayim) and I have also given gifts to all that are with thee, and I have also given Avraham sheep, cattle, man and maidservants. However, my above quoted interpretation is better. It means that Avraham is a covering of the eyes to thee, before the servants that you had prior to coming here and before the servants that I have given you. class="footnote">According to I.E. the root of ve-nokhachat is yod, caf, chet, meaning to chasten, show (Weiser). For alternate interpretations of I.E.’s comment on this verse, see Filwarg.
Similarly ve-et kol (and before all men) means, and before all men Avraham is your covering of the eyes.

According to this interpretation only ve-nokhachat (and she was chastened) are the words of Moshe. Hence the vav of ve-nokhachat is a connective vav as it is normally. Saadiah Gaon says that ve-nokhachat comes from nokhach (in front of). However, he is wrong.

And they bore children. That is, Avimelech’s wife and maidservants. It does not refer to Avimelech. The following are similar: and shed the blood of war in peace (Melachim I 2:5); He spoke unto them in the pillar of cloud (Tehillim 99:7); These are the sons of Adah (Bereshit 36:12); for whom I have served thee (Bereshit 30:26), and the father of Avraham, and the father of Nachor; and they served other gods (Yehoshua 24:2). That and they bore children does not apply to Avimelech is obvious from the fact that Avimelech per se is omitted from the verse which follows, For Hashem had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Avimelech, because of Sarah Avraham’s wife (v. 18). I dwell on this point because there are commentators who insist that Avimelech’s bowels were closed up and he could not eliminate.

However, the presence of the phrase all the wombs (v. 18) clearly refutes their interpretation. The term va-yeledu (and they bore children) is used when referring to women even though it is a masculine form. Compare, va-yechemu ha-tzon (and the flocks conceived) (Bereshit 30:39).
At the set time of which God had spoken to him. The reference is to the angel who had asked, Where is Sarah thy wife? The same angel also returned to Avraham, for he had promised to do so.
[Yitzchak.] Hashem never added any letter to Yitzchak’s name; neither did He ever change it, for Hashem Himself commanded Avraham to call his son Yitzchak.
Making sport. Yishmael was acting as a boy is wont to act. Sarah was jealous because he was older than her son.
On account of his son. Odot means account of.

And a bottle of water. Chemet (bottle) is a vessel. It is possibly made out of skin or wood. Chamatekha (thy venom) in That puttest thy venom (chamatekha) thereto (Chavakuk 2:15) is analogous. Many are amazed at Avraham’s behavior. They ask, how could Avraham chase his son out of his house? How could he send away mother and child empty handed? Where was his kindness? However, I am amazed at those who are amazed at Avraham, for Avraham acted according to Hashem’s dictates. Had he acted contrary to Sarah’s wishes and given money to Hagar, then he would have transgressed Hashem’s command. However, ultimately, after Sarah’s death, he gave gifts to Yishmael’s children.

Bread and a bottle of water. He gave the bread and bottle of water to Hagar and placed them upon her shoulder. He then told her, “Take your son with you,” and he sent her away. It is possible that Avraham gave Hagar some gold and silver, although this is not mentioned in Scripture. Avraham at that time lived in Gerar. He gave Hagar enough bread and water to last her till she reached Beer Sheva. However, Hagar did not know the way and strayed in the wilderness of Beer Sheva. Yishmael became ill from lack of water. She took him to her bosom and when she saw that he was dying of thirst, she cast him under one of the shrubs.
Under one of the shrubs. One of the trees.
As it were a bowshot. Ki-metachave (as it were a shot) is not found elsewhere in the Bible. Its definition is known. It means the distance an arrow travels after being shot.

An archer. Compare, Call together the archers (rabbim) against Bavel (Yirmiyahu 50:29). Although roveh (archer) in our verse and rabbim (archers) (in Yirmiyahu 50:29) come from different roots, they mean the same thing. We find a similar case with the words sarar and sarah (ruled over), also the words ravah and ravav, both of which mean increased.
Archer. Kashat (archer) is an adjective. Compare, gannav (thief).
Have I even here seen him that seeth me? The angel first appeared to her here.
That thou wilt not deal falsely with me. Tishkor (thou wilt deal falsely) is a kal. This is the only place in the Bible that this word appears in the kal.
My son’s son. Nechdi is to be rendered the son of my son.
What mean these. Hennah (these) is feminine.
By themselves. Levaddanah (by themselves) is spelled with a heh at the end of the word. This is the only place in Scripture where the word is so written.

A witness. Le-edah means a witness. It should be noted that the word for oath (shevu’ah) comes from the word for seven (shivah). I will elaborate on this point in my comments on the term oh hishavah shevu’ah (or sweareth an oath).
A tamarisk-tree. Eshel (a tamarisk tree) is a tree. The word va-yitta (and he planted) which precedes it is also proof of this.

That God did prove Avraham. Some say that the word nissah (did prove, tested) is a variation of nissa (lifted up), with the sin replacing the samekh and the heh replacing the alef. However, the plain meaning of the entire chapter contradicts this interpretation. The word nissah is thus to be taken literally. The philosophers teach that there are two kinds of knowledge, knowledge of events prior to their occurrence, and knowledge of what is presently in existence. The latter is the meaning of God did prove, and for now I know (v. 12). Saadiah Gaon says that did prove means that God tested Avraham in order to demonstrate his piety to mankind; furthermore, he interprets for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man (v. 12) to mean that now I have made known to all that thou art a God-fearing man. But didn’t Saadiah know that even Avraham’s young men were not present when he bound Yitzchak and placed him on the altar? Others say that and offer him there for a burnt offering is to be interpreted as: bring him up to the mountain; this will be considered as if you brought him up as a burnt offering. However, Avraham did not understand his prophetic vision and hurried to sacrifice Yitzchak. God then told him, “I did not ask you to slay Yitzchak.” Still others say that God told Avraham: act as if you were bringing him up as a burnt offering. We find a similar occurrence in connection with the prophet Yirmiyahu, who was commanded to Go unto the house of the Rechavim…and give them wine to drink (Yirmiyahu 35:2). Now these geonim offered the above interpretations because they held that it is not possible that God would issue a command and then take it back. However, they overlooked the fact that God took the firstborn to serve Him and after a year replaced them with the Leviyim. In reality all questions are removed by Scripture’s first stating that God did prove Avraham. The reason God tested Avraham was in order to reward him.

The meaning of for now I know that (v. 12) is the same as and if not, I will know (Bereshit 18:21). I will also explain, if Hashem who knows all hidden things will help me, the secret meaning of this term in my comments on I know thee by name (Shemot 33:12).

Upon one of the mountains. The temple was later built on this mountain. This is explicitly stated in Scripture: So Shlomo built the house on Mount Moriyah. It was not a very tall mountain. The threshing floor of Aravnah the Yevusi was on it.
And he cleaved the wood for the burnt-offering. And placed them on his ass.
On the third day. That he set out from Beer Sheva.

Some ask, how could Avraham say, and (we will) come back to you (v. 5)? Others answer them by saying that Avraham intended to return with Yitzchak’s bones, and he disguised his intentions so that his young men would wait for him till he returned and Yitzchak would not know what was about to happen and flee. Our sages, of blessed memory, say that Yitzchak was thirty-seven years old at the time of his binding. If this be a tradition, we will accept it. However, from a strictly logical point of view it is unacceptable. If Yitzchak was an adult at this time, then his piety should have been revealed in Scripture and his reward should be double that of his father for willingly having submitted himself to be sacrificed. Yet Scripture says nothing concerning Yitzchak’s great self-sacrifice. Others say that Yitzchak was five years old at the time of his binding. This, too, is unacceptable, since Yitzchak carried the wood for the sacrificial pyre. It thus appears logical to assume that Yitzchak was close to thirteen years old and that Avraham overpowered him and bound him against his will. Proof of this can be seen from the fact that Avraham hid his intention from Yitzchak and told him, Elokim will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son (v. 8). Avraham knew that if he said, “You are to be the burnt-offering,” Yitzchak would quite possibly have fled.
Avraham, Avraham. The repetition of the name expresses urgency.

Behind him a ram caught in the thicket. Avraham beheld a ram after (achar) it had been caught in the thicket by its horns. If the chet of ne’echaz (caught) is vocalized with a kamatz, then the word “was” is missing from the text and the meaning of the phrase is, after it was yet caught in the thicket. There are many other similar instances. Others say that achar is connected to And Avraham lifted up his eyes. But if this were so, the word achar would have been followed by ken or zot, as is the case whenever the word achar (after) indicates a pause.
[In the Mount where Hashem is seen.] The meaning of this clause can be ascertained in my comments on These are the words (Devarim 1:1).
By myself have I sworn. By Myself indicates a great and eternal oath.
Because. Ya’an (because) is similar in meaning to anah (testify or bear witness). The meaning of the term is: this act will testify and bear witness.
The gate of his enemies. Cities surrounded by walls having gates.
Because. Ekev (because) means a reward that is granted at the end.

So Avraham returned. Yitzchak is not mentioned because he was under Avraham’s care. Those who say that Avraham slaughtered Yitzchak and left him on the altar and following this Yitzchak came to life are contradicting Scripture.
Behold, Milkah, she also hath borne. This is stated to inform us of Rivkah’s pedigree.

The life of. The word life (chayyim) is always encountered in the plural. We never find it in the singular. [A HUNDRED AND SEVEN AND TWENTY YEARS.] Hebrew usually first lists the larger numbers and then the smaller ones. But we also find the opposite, an example being Scripture’s enumeration of Yaakov’s years (Bereshit 47:28).

Kiriath-Arba. Arba was the name of one of the great men of the Anakim. The identification of Arba with Avraham is homiletical, as Avraham was not of that race. When Sarah died Avraham was elsewhere; hence Scripture states, and Avraham came.
And to weep for her. The word livkotah is to be rendered to weep for her. And bewail her father (Devarim 21:13) is similar.
Before his dead. This alludes to the body. [SAYING.] The explanation of this term is found elsewhere in this commentary.
I am a stranger. When the word stranger (ger) stands by itself, it refers to a transient stranger.

And a sojourner (ve-toshav) means a resident stranger. Avraham said to them, “I am a sojourner among you. We are all mortal, I do not have a possession (achuzah) i.e., an inherited or bought piece of land for use as a burial plot.”
My Lord. Not our lord. One man spoke. He employed the term my lord because it is impolite to include others when one is speaking as a subordinate.
A mighty prince. Because thou art a prophet. The term elohim (mighty) is used in the sense of great.
Shall withhold. Yikhleh means shall withhold. It can be spelled either with a heh or an alef.

[And bowed down.] I have given the grammatical explanation of this word in The Book of Foundation. Those who say that Avraham bowed down to God speak nonsense. Scripture explicitly states that Avraham bowed to the children of Chet. Bowing means a bending of the head. It is a way of showing reverence. Moshe also bowed before his father-in-law.
The cave of Machpelah. A cave within a cave.
For the full price. The opposite of male (full) is chaser (lacking).
Nay. Not so, my lord, only hear me.
Before the people of the land. Avraham bowed before Efron in the presence of the people of the land in order to honor him.
But if thou wilt, I pray thee, hear me. If you will do this I pray thee, hear me. Or it may mean, if you will do this, I pray thee, when I will give the price of the field, take it of me.
Current money with the merchant. Merchants accept only the best currency.

Were made sure. The field was made sure and passed permanently into Avraham’s possession. This verse and the one that preceded it are to be read as one verse. Similarly the verse opening with I am a stranger and a sojourner (v. 4) and the verse which precedes it are to be read as one verse. The ten pairs of verses that Saadiah Gaon listed as being in reality one verse are in fact not to be read as one verse.
[In the presence of the children of Chet.] The local inhabitants.
[Before all that went in at the gate of his city.] Those who happened to be passing by.

And after this, Avraham buried Sarah his wife. After the burial of Sarah the field was made sure as a burial ground possession belonging to Avraham and his descendants. Scripture tells of the purchase of the field of Machpelah to teach us of the superiority of the land of Yisrael over all countries, both for the living and the dead. Moreover, it informs us that Hashem’s word to Avraham that he would possess the land as an inheritance was fulfilled.

And the Lord had blessed Avraham in all things. With length of days, wealth, honor and sons, these being all the things that men desire to have. If the interpretation that Avraham had a daughter named Bakkol were correct, then Scripture should have read: and the Lord blessed Avraham “with” Bakkol.

Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh. Some say that my thigh alludes to Avraham’s circumcised member. However, if this were the case, then Avraham should have made him swear by the covenant of circumcision, and not by the Lord. I believe that it was customary in those days for a person to place his hand under the thigh of his master, its meaning being, “If you are subject to my authority, place your hand under my thigh.” The lord then sat on his servant’s hand. By doing so the servant, as it were, said to the master, “My hand is under your authority to do your will.” This custom is still followed in Hodu.
[The Elokim of heaven and the Elokim of the earth.] Elokim is so described in our verse because it is ordained in heaven who here on earth will be united in matrimony. This thing is a secret.
Of the Kenaani. This includes all of the eleven Kenaani peoples.
But thou shalt go unto my country. To Charan where he had once dwelt.
And to my kindred. Ur of the Chaldees.
Peradventure. Ulai (peradventure) has many meanings in Scripture. If so (ulai) be it yield, strangers shall swallow it up (Hoshea 8:7), is similar.

The heh of he-hashev (must I needs bring back) is vocalized with a segol because the heh of the hifil which follows it is vocalized with a kamatz. If the first heh of he-hashev were vocalized with a pattach, it would be difficult to pronounce both hehs in succession.

[Beware.] When the word hishamer (beware) is penultimately accented it is related to the word shemirah (watching, guarding). However, when it is ultimately accented it is related to the word shemarim (lees). Compare, hishamer (keep calm) in Keep calm (hishamer), and be quiet (Is. 7:4), which has the same basic meaning as shemarav (his lees) in And he hath settled on his lees (shemarav) (Yirmiyahu 48:11).
He will send his angel before thee. This is a prayer. If it were a prophecy Avraham would not have said, And if the woman be not willing to follow thee (v. 8).
Thou shalt not bring my son back thither. He must remain in the land of Yisrael. Avraham said, thou shalt not bring my son back because he (Avraham) was the root.
And he made the camels to kneel down. He made them kneel upon their knees.
Send me, I pray thee. Its meaning is, prepare for me what I desire. Because Hashem thy Elokim sent me (Bereshit 27:20) is similar.

She that thou hast appointed. The servant relied on the efficacy of the prophet’s prayer. He was certain that Hashem accepted it and sent an angel, the latter being Hashem’s very own messenger, to help him by appointing a damsel in a dream. The servant reasoned that there was no family as charitable as his master’s. Many are perplexed because they say that the servant expressed his request improperly. I, however, do not see anything wrong in what he said, for had it been another damsel, one not of Avraham’s family, who offered to give him drink and water his camels, he would have left her and nothing would have been lost, for the verse and said; Whose daughter art thou means he had previously said, before he gave the ring and bracelets to Rivkah, whose daughter art thou ? Scripture similarly states, And I asked her, and said: Whose daughter art thou? And she said: The daughter of Betuel…And I put the ring upon her nose, and the bracelets upon her hands (v. 47). The sum of the matter is the servant prayed that Hashem would appoint for Yitzchak a young lady from the family of his master, the sign of Hashem’s choice being that the damsel would act graciously as a woman of noble character should. Hashem heard his prayer. However, the case of Jonathan is totally different.

Neither had any man known her. It is extremely unlikely that Scripture speaks of abnormal intercourse. The verse rather refers to a certain intercourse method wherein it is possible to sleep with a virgin and even to impregnate her without deflowering her. However, it is unseemly to describe how this can be done.

And the man looked steadfastly on her. Mishta’eh (looked steadfastly) means the same as mishtomem (astonished, awe-struck). It comes from the same root as sha’u and tisha’eh (waste) in Until cities be waste (sha’u) (Is. 6:11), and And the land become utterly waste (tisha’eh shemamah) (Is. 6:11).

The meaning of lah (on her) is because of her. Then Daniel…was appalled (eshtomam) for a while (Daniel 4:16) is similar. The tav of mishta’eh is not part of the root of the word but is the sign of the hitpa’el conjugation. It is like the tav of nitra’eh in let us look (nitra’eh) one another in the face (Melachim II 14:8). Mishta’eh definitely does not come from the root shin, tav, heh (drink).
A golden ring. Nezem (ring) can refer either to a nose ring or to an earring. The one worn on the nose is attached by a string which is tied around the forehead.
Half a shekel. Beka means half a shekel. It comes from the same root as nivka (was cleft).

And two bracelets. Tzemidim (bracelets) comes from the same root as tzamid (cover of a vessel) in covering (tzamid) close-bound (Bamidbar 19:15). A bracelet is called a tzamid because each bracelet worn on the hand is made up of two parts. The form of this ornament is well known.
To lodge in. La-lin (to lodge in) is in the hifil. If it were a kal it would read la-lun.
And provender. Mispo (provender) is a general term for cattle feed. The Bible could have used barley in its place.
And there was set. Va-yusam (and there was set) is in the hofal. It is like va-yushav (brought) in And Moshe and Aharon were brought (va-yushav) (Shemot 10:8).

Some say that the statement I am Avraham’s servant is connected to I will not eat, the meaning of the verse being: I am Avraham’s servant and there are certain foods which we are prohibited from eating. However, I believe that the meaning of the servant’s words are self-evident.
Then shalt thou be clear from my oath. The servant did not say, from my shevu’ah (oath). What he meant was, “I fear my master and his curse.”
Kindly. Chesed (kindly) denotes an act which one is not obligated to perform.
And truly. Emet (truly) denotes keeping the promise to deal kindly. The word emet comes from the same root as emunah (steadfastness). The tav of emet is the sign of the feminine.
As Hashem hath spoken. As Hashem hath decreed. By the word of Hashem were the heavens made (Tehillim 33:6) is similar. On the other hand, it may mean: as Hashem hath appointed in a dream.

Precious things. Migdanot (precious things) comes from the same root as megadim (precious) (Cant. 4:13). On the other hand, it may mean expensive garments. In the latter case the nun of migdanot is part of its root, and the word migdanot follows the paradigm of mitpachot (cloaks).

And her brother and her mother said. They received the gifts and Betuel was silent. It is possible that Lavan was wiser and more respected than his father, for we find, Then Lavan and Betuel answered (v. 50).
And her nurse. In former days.
And they rode upon the camels. That the servant brought with him.

And went his way. Va-yelakh (and went his way) is vocalized with a pattach rather than a kamatz even though it closes a verse, the reason for this being that this word is normally vocalized with a segol, and a vowel cannot go up two steps. The same principle applies to the word va-yomar (and he said).
The meaning of And the servant took Rivkah, and went his way is that he took Rivkah under his personal care until Yitzchak came up toward them and did not experience any hardship in caring for her.

And Yitzchak came from the way of beer-lahai-roi. Be'er Lachai Roi has two names. Others say that ba mi-bo (came from the way) means came from the inside of. They similarly explain the word mi-bo in Every house is shut up, that none may come in (mi-bo) (Is. 24:10). However, I believe that mi-bo is an infinitive and ba mi-bo be’er-la-chai-ro’i means came from the way leading to Be'er Lachai Roi.
For he dwelt in the land of the south. For at the time he dwelt there (in the Negev). The latter is in the southern part of the land of Yisrael.
And Yitzchak went out to meditate. The word la-su’ach (to meditate) means to walk among the trees.

At the eventide. Close to sunset. The opposite of li-fenot erev (at the eventide) is lifnot boker (before the dawning of the day). I will give a full explanation of these terms in the Torah portion Ki Tetze.

[She alighted from the camel.] Of her own free will. Compare, he fell upon his face (Bamidbar 16:4). What is reported in the following verse took place before, for the meaning of va-tomer el ha-eved is: And she had said unto the servant.
And covered herself. Va-titkas (and covered herself) is in the hitpa’el. The first tav is the sign of the third person feminine, and the second tav, the tav of the hitpa’el.

Into his mother Sarah’s tent. This is short for the tent, tent of Sarah his mother. Even the prophecy of Oded the prophet (Divrei Hayamim II 15:8) and Thy throne given of Elokim (Tehillim 45:7) are similar.

Keturah. Keturah is not to be identified with Hagar because Scripture explicitly states, But unto the sons of the concubines (pilagshim), that Avraham had, Avraham gave gifts (v. 6). The meaning of pilegesh (concubine) is a handmaid. This term cannot refer to a male. We can explain upon concubinage (Yechezkel 23:20) as referring to females.
Asshurim. Some say that asshurim means those who know the roads and letushim, those who see from afar. However, I believe that asshurim and letushim are proper nouns and not adjectives.
Gifts. He gave them money.

Eastward. Kedemah (eastward) means unto the East country. And it shall come to pass, that the nation and the kingdom which will not serve him, Nevuchadnetzar King of Bavel (Yirmiyahu 27:8) is similar. East means east of the land of Yisrael. Others say that kedemah (eastward) means to the place where the son of Yishmael dwelt. The first of these two interpretations is the correct one.

[And Avraham expired.] Expired refers to a death wherein the soul leaves the body in a moment, without pain or delay. Proof of this is he (Yaakov) gathered up his feet unto the bed and then immediately expired (Bereshit 49:33). Every expiration (gevi’ah) is a death, but not every death is an expiration (gevi’ah). Hence Scripture states, with regard to those who perished in the flood, And all flesh expired (Bereshit 7:21).
The meaning of, and (Avraham) died is that he died at a ripe old age.

And was gathered to his people. Some say that this refers to the soul of life which, even while functioning in the body, is a separate entity. When it separates from the body it returns to its source. Others say that and was gathered to his people is a mere idiom. One who follows in the footsteps of his ancestors is said, as it were, to be joining them. But thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace (Bereshit 15:15) is similar.
And by their encampments. Tirotam (encampments) means palaces. Compare, a turret of silver (tirat kasef) (Cant. 8:9).

According to their nations. We find Scripture employing ummot (nations) and ummim (nations), both of which are vocalized with a shuruk. The lamed of le-ummatam (according to their nations) is a preposition, similar to the lamed of le-goyehem (after their nations). It is not the same as the lamed of ba-le’ummim (upon the peoples) (Tehillim 149:7) which is a root letter like the lamed of le’om (people) in And the one people (u-le’om) shall be stronger than the other people (mi-le’om) (v. 23). Whether spelled with a lamed or not, it has the same meaning. However, they come from different roots.
Over against all his brethren. Zimram and Yokshan.

He did settle. The meaning of nafal (fell) is that his portion or his lot fell among his brethren. Or it refers to the fact that most of the Yishmeelim journeyed from place to place. In this case nafal is like nofel in Thou fallest away (nofel) to the Kasdim (Yirmiyahu 37:13). However, this is a bit far-fetched in view of the fact that his brethren were in the east (v. 6), and Mitzrayim and Ashur are west of the land of Yisrael. It is possible that this verse deals with Yishmael’s death. He died during the lifetime of his brethren, after he fell. We do not know the cause of Yishmael’s death.

And these. After recording the generations of Yishmael, Scripture returns to record the progeny of Yitzchak, Esav and Yaakov. Some say that Avraham begot Yitzchak means that Yitzchak resembled his father, and all who looked upon him could tell that he was Avraham’s son. Others say that holid (begot) means raised and brought up, as in were born (yulledo) upon Yosef’s knees (Bereshit 50:23). This interpretation is substantiated by And he sent them away from Yitzchak his son (v. 6).
Of paddan. Padan means a field. It has the same meaning in Arabic.
The sister of Lavan. Lavan is mentioned because he was better known and more revered than her father. Elisheva…the sister of Nachshon (Shemot 6:23), is similar.
And Yitzchak entreated. Va-yetar (entreated) is in the kal. However, hatiru (entreat) in Entreat Hashem (Shemot 8:4) is in the hifil. Its meaning is that Yitzchak appeased Hashem with his prayers.
And the Lord let himself be entreated. Va-ye’ater means and He was appeased. It is a nifal.

And the children struggled together. Va-yitrotzatzu (and they struggled) comes from the word that means running. The tzadi is doubled. Its parallel is found in They run to and fro (yerotzetzu) like the lightnings (Nachum 2:5). The Bible refers to the fetuses as children because that is what they ultimately became. And stripped the naked of their clothing (Iyov 22:6) is similar. Rivkah asked women who had children if they had had a similar experience. They responded that they did not.
Rivkah then said, if it, namely, the manner and custom of pregnancy, be so as they said, wherefore do I undergo such an abnormal pregnancy.
And Hashem said unto her. Via a prophet, or through Avraham himself, for Avraham did not pass away until her sons were fifteen years of age.
The elder. Elder is the subject. A son honoureth his father (Malachi 1:6) is similar. I will explain our verse later.

Twins. The root letter alef is missing in the word tomim (twins). Tomim in this regard is like the word sheritikha (release thee) in Verily I will release thee (sheritikha) for good (Yirmiyahu 15:11), the meaning of which is: I will deal well with thy last years (she’erit).
[Ruddy.] The yod of admoni (ruddy) is superfluous. It is similar to the yod of akhzari (cruel).

[Like a mantle.] Ke-adderet (like a mantle) is not in the construct with se’ar (hairy). The verse is to be read as follows: all over hairy, like a mantle. However, others say that ke-adderet is in the construct with se’ar.

And they called his name. Those who saw him called him thus. The name Esav possibly connotes a unique occurrence (ma’aseh). This birth was extremely wondrous. Every human being leaves the womb in a placenta which covers him. However, in this instance the two placentas opened simultaneously.
And his name was called. Someone, or Yitzchak his father, called him Yaakov.

A cunning hunter. Esav was constantly practicing deception, for most animals are trapped through trickery. Yaakov was his antithesis, because he was a man of integrity. They also differed in that Esav was a man of the field and Yaakov a man dwelling in tents. It is possible that the meaning of dwelling in tents is like dwell in tents and have cattle (Bereshit 4:20).
Because he did eat of his venison. He brought him game to eat.
And he was faint. Ayef (faint) means hungry and thirsty, as in be-eretz ayefah (in a weary land) (Is. 32:2).
Let me swallow. This is the only place in Scripture where the word, haliteni (let me swallow) is encountered. Its meaning is feed me.

Nazid (pottage) means a cooked dish. However, va-yazed (sod) is an ayin vav. They are two roots with one meaning. Yadon (shall abide) in My spirit shall not abide (yadon) (Bereshit 6:3) and nedanah (the sheath thereof) (Divrei Hayamim I 21:27) are similar.

Sell me. Mikhrah (sell me) is vocalized with a chirik, like shilchah (send) in Send (shilchah) the lad (Bereshit 43:8) and shikhvah (lie) in Lie (shikhvah) with me (Bereshit 39:7. The birthright refers to the double share of the father’s wealth which belongs to the first born. Others maintain that the first born is always superior to his younger siblings in that they must rise before him and serve him as a son serves his father.
[Behold, I am at the point to die.] He was daily exposed to danger when he went out hunting, as an animal might kill him. Thus there was a possibility that he would predecease his father.

So Esav despised. Esav also despised the birthright because he saw that his father had no wealth. Many are amazed at this because Avraham left Yitzchak a vast amount of money?” Have they never seen a man very rich in his youth and poor in his old age? Proof that Yitzchak was poor is the fact that he loved Esav because of his need. Had there been ample food in Yitzchak’s house and Esav the honorable one in his father’s sight, he would not have sold his birthright for a dish of food. Furthermore, why did Yitzchak have to tell Esav, Bring me venison (Bereshit 27:7), if he had savory meat at home for his daily meals? Additionally, why did Yaakov not have choice garments and why didn’t Rivkah give Yaakov gold and silver for his journey (when he fled to Charan), seeing that Yaakov was so poor that he had to say, “If Hashem will…give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on” (Bereshit 28:20). Also, why did Rivkah, who loved him so much, not send him money in view of the fact that he was so impoverished that he had to tend Lavan’s flock? As to the verse which states, And the man waxed great…And he had possessions of flocks, and possessions of herds, and a great household (Bereshit 26:13, 14), it refers to the period prior to Yitzchak’s old age. Now, those who are intellectually blind think that wealth is a great distinction for the righteous. However, the prophet Eliyahu shows that the opposite is the case. They further ask, why did Hashem withhold wealth from Yitzchak? Let them tell us why Hashem withheld sight from Yitzchak’s eyes. Let them not put us off with a poor answer based upon a Midrashic homily, for there is a secret meaning in the matter and we must not probe into it, for the thoughts of Hashem are deep and beyond the ken of man. Similarly others say, behold Yitzchak had sheep, for Rivkah told Yaakov, Go now to the flock (Bereshit 27:9). However, it is possible that he had a few sheep remaining. It is also possible that Go now to the flock means go to the place where sheep are sold.

And kept my charge. Mishmarti (my charge) is a general term for all that Avraham was obligated to observe from the commandments (mitzvot), statutes (chukkim) and laws (torot). It is possible that the commandments spoken of in our verse refer to Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred etc. (Bereshit 12:1), and Take now thy son…even Yitzchak…and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains etc. (Bereshit 22:2).

The statutes spoken of in our text pertain to the works of Hashem that a man should uphold. These statutes are based on logic. I will elaborate on this term (chukkim) in my comments on the verse dealing with the prohibition of wearing a garment of two kinds of stuff mingled together (Vayikra 19:19). The torot (laws) mentioned in our verse relate to Avraham’s circumcision of himself, his children and his servants. I will fully explain the meaning of the terms torah and mitzvah in my comments on the verse and the law and the commandment (Shemot 24:12).
And Yitzchak dwelt in Gerar. Yitzchak did as Hashem had commanded him.
Of his wife. The word le-ishto (of his wife) should be rendered: about his wife. We find a similar meaning for this word in that men say not of me (li) (Jud. 9:54).

For he feared. Yare (he feared) is a perfect, as is the word zaken (old) in And it came to pass, that when Yitzchak was old (zaken) (Bereshit 27:1). The words “because he said” have been omitted before lest the men of the place should kill me. We find this phrase similarly omitted in for Elokim hath made me fruitful (Bereshit 41:52).

A hundredfold. The word sha’ar means the same as the Rabbinic term shi’ur (estimate, reckon). The meaning of me’ah she’arim (a hundredfold) is that Yitzchak was blessed in that the earth produced one hundred times more than what he sowed was estimated to produce. The word she’arim comes from the same root as sha’ar in For as one that hath reckoned (sha’ar) within himself (Mishlei 23:7).
And grew. Ve-gadel (and grew) is a perfect.
And a great household. Yitzchak had man and maidservants to serve him. Avuddah (household) is an adjective. On the other hand, it may be a noun following the paradigm of segullah (treasure).
[Wells.] When the word be’erot is in the construct it can be vocalized in one of two ways.
Living water. Water that is always bursting forth.
Esek. This word is not encountered elsewhere in Scripture. However, its meaning can be ascertained from Rabbinic literature.

Digged. Va-yikhru means digged. Kariti, in in my grave which I have digged (kariti) for me (Bereshit 50:5); yikhreh in or if a man shall dig (yikhreh) a pit (Shemot 21:33); and koreh, in whoso diggeth (koreh) a pit shall fall therein (Mishlei 26:27), are similar.
Betwixt us. Our verse contains two synonymous plurals in succession.

Beer Sheva. There were two reasons why the city was so called. On the other hand, it is possible that this Beer Sheva is not to be identified with the Beer Sheva previously mentioned (Bereshit 21:28-31).
Judith. Judith is a proper name. She did not bear Esav any children.
Basmat. Basmat is to be identified with Adah. She had two names. There are hundreds of similar instances in Scripture.

A bitterness of spirit. Each one of Esav’s wives was a morat ru’ach (bitterness of spirit) to Yitzchak and Rivkah. Some say that morat (bitterness) is similar to the word moreh (rebellious) in If a man have a stubborn and rebellious (moreh) son (Devarim 21:18). However, I believe that morat comes from the same root as marah (bitter) in bitter (marah) as wormwood (Mishlei 5:4). Indeed, it is explicitly written, and Esav saw that the daughters of Kenaan pleased not Yitzchak, his father (Bereshit 28:8). The account of Esav’s wives was recorded so that Bnei Yisrael would keep themselves from taking Kenaani women.
Behold now. The word na means now.

Thy weapons. Khelekha (thy weapons) is possibly a general term, the particulars being thy quiver and thy bow. Telyekha (thy quiver) is a sheath hanging from its bearer wherein arrows are placed. On the other hand, khelekha may refer to a sword. However, in this case a conjunctive vav should have been placed in front of telyekha. Nevertheless, it does not refute the latter interpretation, for we find a similar instance in Adam, Shet, Enosh (Divrei Hayamim I 1:1).
And Rivkah heard. Shoma’at (heard) should be translated, “was listening.”
Before my death. Before I die.

Hairy. The word sa’ir means hairy. The opposite of sa’ir is chalak (smooth) (v. 11). Someone without hair on his body is possibly so called (chalak) because all parts of his body (chalakav) are the same.
Will feel me. Yemusheni (will feel me) is similar to yesubeni (compasseth me about) (Tehillim 49:6). It belongs to those roots whose second and third letters are the same.
As a mocker. The root of ki-metate’a (as a mocker) is doubled. It comes from the same root as to’eh (err). The meaning of ki-metate’a is: as one who misleads his fellow man.

Upon me be thy curse. Don’t be afraid that your father might curse you. If he does, the curse will be upon me, not on you. This is the way women talk. However, Saadiah Gaon explained Upon me be thy curse to mean: it is upon me to remove the curse.

[I am.] Some say, Heaven forbid that a prophet should lie. We must therefore interpret Yaakov’s words to his father as follows: I am who I am and Esav is thy first born. Others say that Yaakov quietly said, I am, and then loudly said, Esav is thy first-born. Now these interpretations are nonsence. Prophets are divided into two groups. One group consists of Elokim’s messengers concerning commandments; the other, those who foretell the future. If the latter have to say something that is not quite so, there is no harm done. However, a prophet whose task is to reveal commandments never lies. We thus find that King David, whom Scripture calls the man of Elokim (Divrei Hayamim II 8:14) and who said, The spirit of Hashem spoke by me (Shmuel II 23:2), perverted the truth out of need of the hour when he spoke to Avimelech and said, Of a truth women have been kept from us about these three days, when I came out, the vessels of the young men were holy (Shmuel I 21:6). Also, the prophet Elisha did not speak the truth when he said to Chazael, Go, say unto him, thou shalt surely recover (Melachim II 8:10), even though what he meant was, go say unto him that thou shalt recover from this illness; however, Elokim has shown me that he will be killed. Similarly the prophet Michayhu uttered a vain prayer out of deference to King Achav when he told him, Go up and prosper; and Hashem will deliver it into the hand of the king (Melachim I 22:15). Similarly Daniel said to King Nevuchadnetzar, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee (Daniel 4:16). Those who explain that My lord refers to Elokim are indulging in Midrash. Similarly Avraham said unto Avimelech, And moreover she is indeed my sister (Bereshit 20:12); and unto his young men, and I and the lad will go yonder and we will worship and come back to you (Bereshit 22:5).

And eat of my venison. Okhlah (eat) is similar to zokhrah (remember) in Remember (zokhrah) unto me, O my Elokim, for good, all that I have done for this people (Nechemyah 5:19). The alef of okhlah is a root letter.
That I may feel thee. There is no dagesh in the shin of va-amushekha (that I may feel thee) in order to simplify the enunciation of this word.

And I will eat of my son’s venison. The alef of ve-okhelah (and I will eat) is a first person imperfect prefix. It is vocalized with a cholam to compensate for the missing alef of the root. We find the same in the word omerah in I will say (omerah) unto God my Rock (Tehillim 42:10).

The nun of tevarakhanni (may bless me) (v. 19) receives a dagesh to make up for the missing nun which should have been in our word, as we find in yesovevenhu (He compassed him about) (Devarim 32:10) and similarly in yeshacharuneni (they will seek Me) (Hoshea 5:15).
[And kissed him.] When the word kiss is followed by a lamed it means to kiss upon the hand, shoulder or neck; when it is not followed by a lamed it indicates a mouth to mouth kiss.

And he smelled. The resh of va-yarach (and he smelled) is vocalized with a pattach because it precedes a gutteral. Va-yana (was moved) and va-yanach (and rested), in And his heart was moved (va-yana) (Is. 7:2) and and rested (va-yanach) in all the borders of Mitzrayim (Shemot 10:14), are similar. All of the above come from roots whose middle letter is a vav.

See. Yitzchak said this to himself. The garments gave off a pleasant odor when Yitzchak thought in his heart that it was Esav before him and that Esav had just come in from the field. The garments gave off the scent of trees in blossom since it is possible that this episode took place in the first month.
[Of the dew.] The mem of mi-tal (of the dew) is also to be prefixed to mishmane (of the fat places). Shall I give my first-born for my transgression? (Michah 6:7) is similar.
Thy brethren. The children of the concubines.
Thy mother’s sons. Esav and his children.

Cursed be everyone that curseth thee. Each one of those that will curse you. But the righteous are secure as a young lion (Mishlei 28:1) is similar. There are many other analogous expressions in Scripture. And blessed be everyone that blesseth thee is also similar.
Who then is he. Mi efoh hu (who then is he?) should be interpreted as follows: who is he and where is he? The word efoh (then) is made up of two words.
The vav of va-varakhehu (and have blessed him) is vocalized with a kamatz because va-avarakhehu is a perfect. Had the vav been vocalized with a pattach, then va-avarachehu would be an imperfect.
With guile. He did not speak the truth.
Is not he rightly. Ha-khi is to be rendered as truly. Ha-khi in Thou art truly (ha-chi) my brother (Bereshit 29:15) is similar.
Named. Someone named him Yaakov.

For he hath supplanted me. Va-yakeveni (for he hath supplanted me) is to be rendered: for he hath deceived me. Ve-okbah (in subtlety) in But Yehu did it in subtlety (ve-okbah) (Melachim II 10:19) is similar. It is possible that it comes from the same root as akov (deceitful) in The heart is deceitful (akov) (Yirmiyahu 17:9). Akov is the opposite of mishor (straight).

Reserved a blessing for me. Kept with yourself (etzlekha) a blessing for me. Atzalta (reserved) comes from the same root as ve-atzalti (and I will take) in And I will take (ve-atzalti) of the spirit which is upon thee (Bamidbar 11:17).

Behold, I have made him thy Lord. Via my blessing. Similarly have I given to him (v. 33) also means I have verbally given. Some say that efo (then) spelled with an alef at the end is one word meaning now.

And it shall come to pass when thou shalt break loose. Tarid (thou shalt break loose) has the same meaning as tirdeh (thou shalt rule) (Vayikra 25:43). However, tarid and tirdeh have different roots. Others say that tarid is similar to arid (I cry out) in I cry out (arid) in my complaint (Tehillim 55:3). According to this interpretation the meaning of our clause is: and it shall come to pass when thou shalt cry out, then God will pity you.

That thou shalt shake his yoke. U-farakto (that thou shalt shake) comes from the same root as mefarek (rent) in rent (mefarek) the mountains (Melachim I 19:11). The word mafrakto (his neck) (Shmuel I 4:18) is derived from the same stem. These blessings present a number of great difficulties. If the blessings were prophecies how is it possible for Yitzchak not to know whom he was blessing? The wise men of our generation respond to this problem by explaining that when Yaakov entered the room, Hashem told him, “Bless this one.” However, if this was the case Yitzchak would have told Esav, “Hashem commanded me to bless Yaakov.” Furthermore, if Hashem told Yitzchak to bless Yaakov, why did Yitzchak bless Esav because he cried? Others say that Yitzchak was no prophet and his blessings did not come to pass. However, they are also mistaken. Scripture explicitly tells us, And Hashem appeared unto him (Yitzchak) (Bereshit 26:2, 24). Moreover, King David in referring to the patriarchs says, And do My prophets no harm (Divrei Hayamim I 16:22). Others ask, what efficacy could there be in Yitzchak’s blessings since he thought that he was blessing Esav? The truth of the matter is that Yitzchak was in doubt as to who was really before him. Indeed, he said, The voice is the voice of Yaakov, but the hands are the hands of Esav (v. 22). What Yitzchak did was bless the one in his presence without regard to whether it was Esav or Yaakov, the reason being that both were his sons. Some ask, how could Hashem say (Bereshit 25:23) And the elder shall serve the younger? Similarly how could Yitzchak say, and thou shalt serve thy brother (v. 40)? Saadiah Gaon superficially answers this question by pointing to Scripture’s statement, And Esav took his wives, and his sons, and his daughters, and all the souls of his house, and his cattle, and all his beasts…and went unto a land away from his brother Yaakov (Bereshit 36:6).
