The Rabbinic statement that all dreams follow the interpretation is the opinion of an individual sage.
Its blossoms shot forth. Nitzah (its blossoms) is the same as henetzu (be in flower) in And the pomegranates be in flower (hanetzu) (Cant. 7:13).

And the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes. Hivshilu (brought forth ripe) is the oppposite of boser (sour grapes). Bashal (is ripe) in For the harvest is ripe (bashal) (Yoel 4:13) is similar. The two words are similar even though hivshilu in our verse and bashal belong to different conjugational paradigms.
And pressed them. Va-eschat (pressed) is similar to shochate (slay) in That slay (shochate) the children in the valleys (Is. 57:5). Saadiah Gaon’s interpretation of va-eschat is wrong.
The interpretation of it. Pitrono (the interpretation of it) means its explanation. The term pitrono is not found in Scripture except in reference to a dream.

Some ask, how did Yosef know that the three branches refer to three days and not to three months or three years? Because yom hulledet et paroh (v. 20) possibly means the day on which Paroh was born. For today there are kings who make a party on their birthday and invite their servants and distribute gifts to them. It is also possible that the queen was pregnant. The first interpretation appeals to me.

Shall Paroh lift up thy head. Yissa means shall lift up. In its correct sense, yissa means to lift up by counting. Proof of this is Scripture stating, and he lifted up (va-yissa) the head of the chief butler and the head of the chief baker among his servants (v. 20). I will explain this term in my comments on the Torah portion Ki Tissa (Shemot 30:12).

Thine office. Kannekha means thy previous station, thy place, thy state. Kannekha most likely comes from the same root as ken (a base, a pedestal) (Melachim I 7:29). The word kanno (in his place) in Then shall stand up in his place (kanno) (Daniel 11:20) is analogous.

Out of the land of the Hebrews. I will explain this in my comments on If thou buy a Hebrew servant (Shemot 21:2). When the term hinneh (behold) is found in Scripture following a dream, its meaning is as it were.
Three baskets of white bread. Saadiah Gaon says that chori means white bread, as in the nobles (chore) of Yehudah (Nechemyah 6:17).
Within yet. Be’od (within yet) is to be translated before again. Its meaning is: such a time will not again pass without this happening.
Shall Paroh lift up thy head from off thee. He will lift it up from its place. It means he will remove it or raise it up on a pole.
Birthday. Hulledet (birth) is an infinitive in the hofal.
Unto his butlership. Mashkehu (his butlership) here is a noun. However, mashkehu in when thou wast his butler (mashkehu) (v. 13) is a verb.

Yet did not the chief butler remember Yosef. He did not verbally mention him to Paroh. The words tizkeru (shall ye mention) and zakhar (he remembered), in And the burden of Hashem shall ye mention (tizkeru) no more (Yirmiyahu 23:36) and he remembered (zakhar) Vashti (Est. 2:1), are similar.
But forgot him. In his heart.

And it came to pass at the end of two full years. Scripture does not indicate the point from which these two years are reckoned. And it came to pass at the end of forty years (Shmuel II 15:7), And within threescore and five years (Is. 7:8), and Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year (Yechezkel 1:1) are similar. However, it is possible that Scripture’s point of reckoning is the chief butler’s release from prison or the day that Yosef was put into prison.
[Full.] I have already explained the meaning of yamim (full).
That Paroh dreamed. That is, was dreaming. Compare, And Rivkah heard (Bereshit 27:5).

In the reed-grass. Some say that achu (reed-grass) means a valley with plants. Others say that achu is the name of a certain type of plant and the bet of ba-achu is superfluous. It is similar to the bet of va-merorim in, He hath filled me with bitterness (va-merorim) (Eichah 3:15). According to both of these interpretations achu here and achim in For though he be fruitful among the reed-plants (achim) (Hoshea 13:15) are related and come from one root.
Ears of corn. Shibbolim (ears of corn) is a feminine plural even though it ends in a mem. It is similar to nashim (women) and pilagshim (concubines).
And blasted. U-shedufot kadim means they were blasted by a wind coming from the east for kadim means east. East is so termed because the sun rises there first.
Ha-mele’ot (full) has the same meaning as ha-beri’ot (rank).

That his spirit was troubled. Va-tippa’em (was troubled) is a nifal. It is similar to nifamti in I am troubled (nifamti) and cannot speak (Tehillim 77:5). Others say that both va-tippa’em and nifamti come from the same root as pa’am (anvil) in that smiteth the anvil (pa’am) (Is. 41:7). Its meaning is that his spirit was like a beaten body.
Magicians of. Chartume (magicians of) comes from a quadriliteral root. However, it is possibly an Aramaic or Mitzri word. It means a scientist.
And all the wise men thereof. Men learned in astrology and dream interpretation.
My faults. Even though I will recall my faults.

Paroh was wroth with his servants. I believe that Paroh is an adjective and not a proper name. It is a Mitzri word. It is a title as Chiram in Tzor. Similarly in our day all great Aravi kings are called “prince of the believers.” Hence we find a Paroh in the days of Avraham and a Paroh in the days of Yosef. We also read that a Paroh died and a new Paroh arose. Similarly we find a Paroh in the days of Yirmiyahu. Do you not see that Scripture itself explains that Paroh is a term for the king of Mitzrayim, as evidenced by the terms Paroh Chofra and Paroh Necho, wherein Chofra and Necho are proper nouns. Do not raise any objection from the Midrash concerning Shlomo’s throne, for the king of Mitzrayim did not take it to Mitzrayim. Additional proof is found in the statement of the chief butler, Paroh was wroth, and in Yosef’s statements, Elokim will give Paroh an answer of peace (v. 16); He hath shown unto Paroh (v. 28); and Let Paroh do this (v. 34). It is not in keeping with proper etiquette to mention the king by name.
Me and the chief baker. The word me is mentioned twice in this verse in keeping with Hebrew usage. Compare, and as for me, whither shall I go (Bereshit 37:30).
Each man according to the interpretation of his dream. I have previously explained this.
I was restored. By Paroh. Or its meaning is, Yosef’s word or Yosef’s interpretation restored me and hanged him.
And they brought him hastily. Paroh’s messengers.
And he shaved himself. Someone shaved him.

It is not in me. Biladai (it is not in me) is a compound of two words. It is not in me refers to And I have heard say of thee that when thou hearest a dream thou canst interpret it (v. 15). When Yosef heard Paroh say this he replied, it is not in me, but Elokim will give Paroh an answer of peace via my interpretation. Others say that when Yosef heard Paroh say, thou canst interpret dreams, Jospeh replied, I am not (it is not in me) the interpreter; Elokim is, and He will give the king an answer of peace.

[Will give an answer.] The meaning of ya’aneh (will give an answer) is, He will always provide. Compare, ma’aneh in for Elokim answereth him (ma’aneh) in the joy of his heart (Kohelet 5:19), and ta’aneh in And the earth shall respond (ta’aneh) (Hoshea 2:24). Nevertheless, the word is close to its primary meaning.
[Poor and very ill-favored.] In relating the dream Paroh added the word dallot (poor), and in place of mareh (favored) he used the term to’ar (favored) because their meanings are similar.

But they were still ill-favored. Each one of the kine was ill-favored. Here Paroh expanded in his description of his dream and added that after the ill-favored kine had eaten the fat kine, they were still ill-favored as at the beginning.
Withered. The word tzenumot (withered) is not found elsewhere in Scripture. Its meaning is the same as that of rekot (empty). Others say that tzenumot means images, for that is its meaning in Arabic.

Great plenty. Sava (plenty) is a noun. It is like ra’av (famine). Hence the one who says in his Sabbath prayers u-ve-sova kilkaltanu errs because sova spelled with a vav is an infinitive. The correct way to read this prayer is without a vav, viz., u-ve-sava (and in plenty) kilkaltanu (thou sustained us).
[And the plenty shall not be known in the land.] Yosef based this on but they were still ill-favored as at the beginning (v. 21).

And for that the dream was doubled. Hishanot (was doubled) is a nifal. It comes from the same root as shenayim (two). Its meaning is the dream coming twice, once with kine as its symbol and then with ears of corn as its symbol, also attests that the thing is established by Elokim. Furthermore, the occurrence of the two dreams in one night is proof that Elokim will shortly bring it to pass.

Let Paroh do this. Ya’aseh paro (literally let Paroh do) is short for let Paroh do according to the following council. Or ya’aseh (do) means get, like asah in My power and the might of my hand hath gotten (asah) me this wealth (Devarim 8:17).
And take up the fifth part of the land. Let him buy a fifth of the produce of the land.

And lay up corn. The overseers. Some say that bar (corn) refers to corn in its ears. However, I think that bar is the term applied to the corn after it has been fanned and cleansed. To the one who says that the Mitzri air is damp because of the Yeor and it is impossible for corn to last there for seven years, we reply that it is possible to mix corn with preservatives.

Can we find such a one as this. Nimtza (we find) is a nifal perfect and the meaning of ha-nimtza kha-zeh ish (can we find such a one as this) is, was such a one as this ever found in the world. It is also possible that the nun of nimtza is a first person plural prefix. In this case the word ha-nimtza (can we find) relates to what Paroh said to his servants.
Thou shalt be over my house. Thou shalt be chief over my house.

Shall be ruled. The shin of yishak (shall be ruled) has a dagesh to compensate for the missing nun of neshek (arms), its meaning being Yosef will be commander of the army. Others say that yishak is related to neshikah (kiss). However, the latter is far fetched.

Only in the throne will I be greater than thou. It is known that egdal (I will be greater) is an intransitive verb. The meaning of rak ha-kisse egdal mi-mekka is, I will not be greater than you except for the dignity of the throne. The word gedelani (he grew up with me) in Nay from my youth he grew up with me (gedelani) as with a father (Iyov 31:18) is not a transitive verb but an intransitive verb meaning he grew up with me. The juxtaposition of an intransitive verb (egdal) with the direct object (kisse) is found elsewhere in Scripture. Compare, For ye shall be as a terebinth whose leaf fadeth (ke-elah novelet aleha) (Is. 1:30); and and ye perish in the way (ve-tovedu derekh) (Tehillim 2:12).
See, I have set thee over all the land. I have set thee above all the land of Mitzrayim.
Vestures of fine linen. I have explained the meaning of shesh (fine linen) in my comments on the Torah portion ve-yikchu li terumah (that they take for me an offering).
A gold chain. Revid (chain) is like marvadim (coverlets) in I have decked my couch with coverlets (marvadim) (Mishlei 7:16).

The second. Mishneh (the second) comes from the same root as shenayim (two). The king is like the numeral one, next comes the mishneh which means second to him, and afterward the shalish (adjutant) which means the same as shilishi (third).
Chariot. A wooden chariot pulled by four horses, as is evidenced by the chariot of Shlomo.

Abrech. Every man called before him, I will bend the knee (avrekh) and I will bow down. The word avrekh is a hifil. However, the word va-yivrakh in and kneeled down (va-yivrakh) upon his knees (Divrei Hayamim II 6:13) is a kal. Both words come from the same root, birkayim (knees). Rabbi Yonah, the Spanish grammarian, said that avrekh is an infinitive, with an alef taking the place of the heh, as we find in the word ashkem in sending them betimes (ashkem) and often (Yirmiyahu 25:4). However, I believe that the alef of ashkem is a first person future prefix.
I am Paroh. I alone am king and aside from you no one is permitted to act freely.
[His foot.] The meaning of his foot is permission to go any place. It may also be a figurative expression. The latter is its correct meaning.

Tzafnat Paneach. If this is a Mitzri word then we don’t know what it means. On the other hand, if this is a Hebrew translation of Yosef’s Mitzri name then we don’t know what Yosef’s Mitzri name was. In the latter case the meaning of paneah is in accordance with Onkelos’ translation, and it is a quadriliteral.
Priest of on. The term kohen (priest) can be applied to one who serves Hashem or to one who serves idols, for I believe that when this term is used in Scripture it means one who ministers.

And Yosef went out. His name went out, as in And thy renown went forth among the nations (Yechezkel 16:14). Or it means he went out and traveled throughout the land and they announced who he was that he might become known.

All the food. All is not to be taken literally, for if it were, then all should have starved to death. All in And all countries came (v. 57) is similar. The meaning of And he gathered up all the food is: and Yosef gathered as much of the food as he could.

For Elokim hath made me forget. Its meaning is, because he said Elokim hath made me forget. Rabbi Yehudah, the first Hebrew grammarian, says that nashani (made me forget) follows the paradigm of channani (dealt graciously with me) (Bereshit 33:11). However, Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen, the Spaniard, says that (in nashani) a pattach has been substituted for the chirik.
And the seven years of famine began. Va-techillenah is a kal and comes from a root whose second and third letters are identical.
In all lands. All the lands adjacent to Mitzrayim.
And Yosef opened all. The storehouses which they had.
And sold unto the Mitzrim. It means he gave corn (shever) to the Mitzrim. Va-yishbor refers to a corn purchase.
To Yosef to buy corn. The clause is inverted and must be understood as: And all the countries came into Mitzrayim to Yosef to buy corn.

Now Yaakov saw. Scripture interchanges the way the senses are referred to because they are all perceived in one central place. Thus Scripture says, See the smell of my son (Bereshit 27:27); and And the light is sweet (Kohelet 11:7). Now Yaakov saw is similar, for afterward Scripture states, Behold I have heard that there is corn in Mitzrayim (v. 2).

Why do you look one upon another. Lammah titra’u (why do you look one upon another) means, don’t show yourselves as having an abundance of food. Or it may mean, do not quarrel with each other, as in Come, let us look one another (nitra’eh) in the face (Divrei Hayamim II 25:17).
And buy for us. Ve-shivru lanu means, and buy corn for us.
Harm. Death.
That sold. Ha-mashbir (that sold) comes from the same root as shever (corn). It means the seller. It is a causative verb.
But made himself strange unto them. Va-yitnakker (but made himself strange) comes from the same root as nokhri (stranger). Its meaning is, he showed himself to be a stranger.
Roughly. Kashot (roughly) is an adjective. Its meaning is rough words. Answereth impudent (Mishlei 18:23) is similar.

And he knew them. When Yosef first saw the group he recognized them as his brothers. He then looked at each one of them and recognized them individually. The latter is the meaning of And Yosef knew his brethren (v. 8).

The nakedness of the land. Nakedness is a figure of speech for shame, since it is customary to hide one’s nakedness because of its unseemliness. Or nakedness refers to secrets, since one’s nakedness is covered. Yosef thus said to them, “You have come to learn the secrets of the land.” I prefer the latter interpretation.
WE. Nachnu (we) is spelled without an alef. This is the correct form of the word.

Upright. Kenim means truthful. It is possible that kenim comes from the same root as ken (so) in So (ken) do, as thou hast said (Bereshit 18:5). Or kenim comes from the same root as ken (truth) in The daughters of Tzelofchad speak right (ken) (Bamidbar 27:7).
And ye shall be bound. He’aseru should be rendered: ye shall be bound. It is similar to u-mot (and die) in and die in the mount (Devarim 32:50).

Famine of your houses. Needed because of the famine of your houses. The meaning of havi’u shever ra’avon batekhem (carry corn for the famine of your houses) is, carry to your houses the corn needed because of the famine.
Verily. Aval (verily) has the same meaning as aval in Verily (aval) Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son (Bereshit 17:19). It means verily (Bereshit 28:16).
The interpreter. Ha-melitz means the interpreter. It is related to melitzah (figure of speech) (Mishlei 1:6).
Yosef imprisoned Shimon because when many sin, the oldest is punished more severely than the others. He did not punish Reuven because he (Reuven) saved him.
Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that the words zahav (gold) and kesef (silver) are never encountered in the plural. However, he forgot that Scripture employs the term kaspehem (money) (v. 25).
[And they laded their asses with their corn.] Which they had bought.

And as one of them opened. Va-yiftach ha-echad means, and one of them opened. The reference is possibly to Reuven, as he was the first born. In this case ha-echad (one of them) means the first in number.
The famine of your houses. Needed for the famine that is in your houses.
All these things. AU these troubles.

[Thou shalt slay.] Some say that thou shalt slay means thou shalt punish. Others say that this was a prayer to Hashem. The sum of the matter is this, if Reuven would have spoken correctly Yaakov would not have ignored him.
Both we. It is Hebrew style to add gam (also) even to the first of a series of items. Compare, Rule over us, also (gam) thou, also (gam) thy son, also (gam) thy son’s son (Jud. 8:22).
Do this. Do according to the following counsel.
Of the choice fruits of the land. Zimrat (choice fruits) refers to all types of praiseworthy things. It comes from the same root as zemirot (songs) (Is. 24:16).
Balm and…spicery. I have previously explained these terms.
Nuts. Batenim does not appear elsewhere in Scripture. Some say it means nuts.
Double. Mishneh means second.
Oversight. Mishgeh (oversight) is a noun whose third root letter is a heh.
[And God Almighty.] This phrase means the one who has the power to do all these things.
If I be bereaved. As I was bereaved by the death of Yosef, I think that I will be bereaved of all my children.
That he may seek occasion against us. Le-hitgolel (that he may seek occasion) comes from the same root as bi-gelal in that for (bi-gelel) this thing (Devarim 15:10).
And fall upon us. As a man falls intentionally upon another and then says you tripped me.

OH. Bi adoni (Oh, my lord) is a supplicatory expression. I believe it is an abridged statement. It is like, bi ani adoni he-avon (upon me, my lord, upon me be the iniquity) (Shmuel I 25:24). Avon (iniquity) here has the same meaning as avon in My iniquity (avoni) is greater than I can bear (Bereshit 4:13). The meaning of bi adoni he-avon is, do to me as you wish but first listen to me.

Hath given you treasure in your sacks. It is possible that someone had a treasure in his house, hid it among the wheat in his storehouse and then forgot about it, and it was placed in your sacks by chance. This must be the case because I have your money.
Into Yosef’s house. The heh at the end of betah (into the house of) means to. The latter is Hebrew style.

Is your father well, the old man. Our verse has a noun (shalom) in place of an adjective (shalem). It is abridged, and should be read as if written, ha-shalom la-avikhem (is your father in peace). Ve-attah shalom (and peace be unto thee) (Shmuel I 25:6) is similar.
And they bowed the head. Va-yikkedu (and they bowed the head) means, and they placed their head to the ground. Thus va-yishtachavu (and made obeisance) means, and they had bowed.
Elokim be gracious unto thee. Yochnekhah (be gracious unto thee) does not fit into any paradigm. Perhaps it differs from the usual paradigms because of the chet which is a guttural.
Yearned. Nikhmeru (yearned) means burned and inflamed, as does nikhmeru (hot) in our skin is hot (nikhmoru) like an oven (Eichah 5:10).
And portions were taken. Masot (portions) means gifts.
Times. Yadot (times) means portions.

As any of theirs. Binyamin’s gifts were five times as great as the gift of any one of the brothers. It is far-fetched to believe that Yosef gave Binyamin five gifts for every gift that he gave to each one of his brothers.
My goblet. Gavi’a (goblet) means a cup.

And whereby he indeed divineth. He used this cup to test you to see if you are thieves. Nachesh (divineth) in our verse is similar to nichashti (I have observed the signs) (Bereshit 30:27). This is also the explanation of know ye not that such a man as I will indeed divine (v. 15). Its meaning is, why were you not afraid to steal my goblet? I placed the goblet before you to test you. I looked aside and you stole it. However, Rabbi Yonah says that bo (whereby) means for it. He interprets nachesh yenachesh bo as: he would indeed inquire of diviners for it. Similarly the meaning of I will indeed divine (v. 15) is: a man in my position has diviners. Some say that the cup had designs on it and that Yosef looked at the cup in the presence of his brothers and announced which of them was the oldest and which one was born next.
[Clear ourselves.] There is a tet in place of the tav of the hitpa’el conjugation in the word nitztaddak (clear ourselves) because the first root letter is a tzadi.
Elokim has found out the iniquity of thy servants. They spoke by way of parable. We committed a sin and it was, as it were, lost and long forgotten, but found today.
Or the iniquity of thy servants means the punishment of thy servants, as in My iniquity is greater than I can bear (Bereshit 4:13).

For thou art even as Paroh. Ki kha-mokha ke-faro means: thou art as the king and the king is as you. This is true in all instances where two cafs are prefixed to two words following each other. Compare, ke-ammi khe-ammekha (my people as thy people) (Melachim II 3:7). The use of two cafs in this manner is an abridged form.
We have a father, an old man. They indicated that their father was an old man because he could have been a relatively young man in view of the fact that the oldest among them was only 45 years old.
That I may set mine eyes upon him. That I may see him.
For if he should leave his father, his father would die. Why didn’t the one who lists the five undecided verses not include our verse and And he drew off his shoe (Rut 4:8) among them.
Surely he is torn in pieces. Proof of which is, And I have not seen him since.
Refrain himself. Le-hitappek (refrain himself) means to bear.
Before all them that stood by him. Its meaning is, until all that stood by him left. Yosef was therefore compelled to call and have them withdrawn.
And he wept aloud. The word reads bi-vechi (wept) even though it is a pausal. Oni (affliction) in I am the man that hath seen affliction (oni) (Eichah 3:1) is similar.
But Elokim. Sent me.
A father. A teacher. Father in he was the father of all such as handle the harp and pipe (Bereshit 4:21) is similar.
Lest thou come to poverty. Tivvaresh (come to poverty) means thou be cut off. Le-horish in to drive out (le-horish) nations (Devarim 4:38) is similar.

That it is my mouth. It is well known that peh (mouth) spelled peh, heh is in the absolute. However, when it appears in the construct the silent heh changes to a silent yod, as in The mouth of (pi) the righteous (Tehillim 37:30). The same form (pi) is also used for the plural, as in But the mouth (pi) of the wicked (Mishlei 10:11). Now when the yod that takes the place of the heh comes together with the yod of the first person pronominal suffix, one of the yods is dropped, as in my mouth (fi) that speaketh. The meaning of my mouth that speaketh unto you is: I speak directly to you in Hebrew without the use of an interpreter.
Neck. Scripture employs both the plural and singular forms for the neck. We also find the word for neck spelled with a nun. However, its alef is never dropped.
Lade. Ta’anu means load. The word meto’ane in thrust through (meto’ane) with the sword (Is. 14:19) is close in meaning to it.
Beasts. Be’irekhem means your cattle. Be’irenu in we and our cattle (u-ve-irenu) (Bamidbar 20:4) is similar.
The fat of the land. Its meaning is shuman ha’aretz (fat of the land).
Changes of raiment. Two garments, each different from the other, two being the minimum for a plural.
[In like manner.] That is, of the finest changes of raiment that were found in Mitzrayim.
Corn. Bar (corn) means grain.
And bread. That is to be taken literally.
And victual. The term mazon (victual) refers to peas, beans, lentils, millet, spelt, figs, raisins and dates, for only these, excluding wheat and barley, are termed mazon.
[See that ye fall not out by the way.] Don’t be angry with each other because of my being sold into slavery.

And his heart fainted. Va-yafag (fainted) comes from the same root as fugat in Give thyself no respite (fugat) (Eichah 2:18). It means his heart stopped and was still. It has the same meaning as and his heart died within him (Shmuel I 25:37). Yaakov reacted in this manner because he didn’t believe them. However, when he saw the wagons, his spirit revived. Do not be surprised at the term his heart stopped for it is the style of the prophets to speak in hyperbole. Compare, neither was there breath left in me (Daniel 10:17).
It is enough; Yosef my son is yet alive. This happiness is enough for me.
To go down. Me-redah (to go down) is an infinitive. Its first root letter is missing. Me-redah is similar to tenah in Whose majesty is rehearsed (tenah) above the heavens (Tehillim 8:2).
[And I will also surely bring thee up again.] This means you will be buried in the land of Yisrael.
And Yosef shall put his hand upon thine eyes. At the time of your death. It is customary for the living to close the eyes of the deceased upon their death.

His daughters. This refers only to Dinah. It is possible that Dinah had maid servants of her own age who grew up with her in Yaakov’s house and who because of Dinah are called Yaakov’s daughters. Yaakov’s “daughters” can be compared to Michal’s “children” (Shmuel II 21:8). The same interpretation is to be given to and his sons’ daughters since Yaakov had only one granddaughter.

The son of a Canaanitish woman. This proves that Yaakov’s sons married Arami, Mitzri, Edomi and Midyani women. Shaul’s mother’s nationality is singled out in order to indicate that Shimon did wrong in marrying a Canaanitish woman. It is for this reason that Scripture records the death of Er and Onan (v. 12). Scripture records their demise in order to indicate that they died because they were the sons of a Canaanitish woman (Bereshit 38:2).
And Naaman. This Naaman was a son of Binyamin. I note this because Binyamin also had a grandson called Naaman (Bamidbar 26:40).
And the sons of Dan: hushim. It is possible that Dan had two sons and one of them died and Scripture did not mention him. It is also possible that the verse employs “sons” for stylistic reasons.

[All the souls of the house of Yaakov, that came into Mitzrayim, were threescore and ten.] An exegate says that three score and ten is a round number, since in fact they numbered sixty-nine. However, this commentator erred, since we find Scripture stating, with regard to Leah’s offspring who numbered thirty-two, all the souls of his sons and daughters were thirty and three (v. 15). The Midrash tries to solve the problem by saying that Yocheved was born between the ramparts when they entered Mitzrayim. However, this, too, presents a problem, viz., why doesn’t Scripture record the great wonder of Yocheved giving birth to Moshe when she was one hundred and thirty years old? Furthermore, why does Scripture note that Sarah was ninety when she bore a son? And as if we didn’t have enough problems with the above, the liturgical poets composed a hymn for Simchat Torah reading, Yocheved my mother will be comforted after me thereby indicating that Yocheved was two hundred and fifty years old at the time of Moshe’s death. As to the Midrash which states that Achiyah the Shiloni lived for hundreds of years, it is an aggadic statement or an individual opinion. I believe that the way to solve our problem is by recognizing the fact that the Bible includes Yaakov among the seventy who came into Mitzrayim and starts the count of the seventy from him. The verse (15) is to be interpreted as if it read: all the souls of his sons and his daughters plus himself were thirty-three. Proof that this is the way to interpret this verse is that Scripture previously states, And these are the names of the children of Yisrael, who came into Mitzrayim, Yaakov and his sons (v. 8). Should one argue and say, “Does not Scripture explicitly state, And all the souls that came out of the loins of Yaakov were seventy souls (Shemot 1:5)? Know that Scripture isn’t concerned with noting that one of the seventy did not come from Yaakov’s loins, as it didn’t bother to leave out Binyamin when it said, These are the sons of Yaakov, that were born to him in Padan Aram (Bereshit 35:26), even though Binyamin was not born there. We have two proofs in our own Torah portion that this is the style of Scripture. First, the Pentateuch states, And these are the names of the children of Yisrael, who came into Mitzrayim, Yaakov and his sons (v. 8). The Torah thus includes Yaakov among the sons of Yisrael. It does so because Scripture speaks of the majority of those who came to Mitzrayim. Secondly, Scripture states, all the souls of the house of Yaakov, that came into Mitzrayim, were three score and ten (Bereshit 46:27). However, Menashe and Efraim did not come into Mitzrayim, they were there to begin with, having been born in Mitzrayim. In the same vein another verse reads, Thy fathers went down into Mitzrayim with three score and ten souls (Devarim 10:22). However, as noted, Menashe and Efraim did not go down to Mitzrayim. This verse is also proof that Yaakov is counted among the seventy, for he had a soul and he was the most important of them all.
And Yosef made ready his chariot. Yosef commanded it ready. So Shlomo built the house, and finished it (Melachim I 6:14), is similar.

For every shepherd is an abomination unto the Mitzrim. This verse shows that in those days the Mitzrim did not eat meat and they did not permit anyone to slaughter sheep. This is still the custom among the Indians. The Mitzrim considered shepherds an abomination because they drank milk. The people of Hodu until this very day do not eat or drink anything derived from a living creature.

In the land of Goshen. The land of Goshen refers to the entire land, the land of Raamses (v. 11) to an area within it. The ayin in Raamses is vocalized with a quiescent sheva. I believe that the city Ra'amses (Shemot 1:11) which is vocalized with a pattach beneath the ayin is not to be identified with the Raamses in which Bnei Yisrael dwelt, for Ra'amses was one of the store cities that Bnei Yisrael built for Paroh.
Rulers over my cattle. Such as horses and mules.

Languished. Va-telah (languished) follows the paradigm of va-teta (and strayed) (Bereshit 21:14). Similarly ke-mitlahle’ah (as a madman) (Mishlei 26:18) is like ki-metate’ah (as a mocker) (Bereshit 27:12). Its meaning is, the land was like a person who has lost his wits.

Was all spent. Va-yittom (was all spent) comes from a root whose second and third letters are identical. It is similar to va-yiddom (stood still) in And the sun stood still (va-yiddom) (Yehoshua 10:13).
Give. According to the rules of Hebrew grammar the heh of havu should have been vocalized with a chataf pattach.
If money fail. Afes (fail) is a perfect. It is similar to the word yare in for he feared (yare) to dwell in Tzoar (Bereshit 19:30).

[Wherefore should we die…both we and our land.] One should not be surprised that the Bible employs the term death to the land. We also find the reverse in Thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all things that are thereon…and Thou givest them all life (Nechemyah 9:6).

Be not desolate. Tesham (be desolate) comes from the same root as tishamenah in and the high places shall be desolate (tishamenah) (Yechezkel 6:6). Tesham follows the paradigm of teda (she will know). The Midrash tells us that the hunger ceased because of Yaakov’s merit. However, it is possible that the hunger lasted for seven years but that it was less intense in the final three years than during the first four years.

And as for the people, he removed them. He uprooted each and every Mitzri from his place. Some say that Scripture speaks of the people of Mitzrayim’s main city. Yosef removed them from the capital to villages so that they would till the soil.
The priests. This is to be rendered as Onkelos does.
And they got them possessions therein. They bought property with title.
And Yaakov lived. The terms put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh and kindly and truly have been explained in the account dealing with Eliezer.

But when I sleep with my fathers. This is a euphemism for death. Or it may mean: bury me not, I pray thee, in Mitzrayim (v. 29), but I will sleep (be buried) with my fathers. The latter will come to pass because thou shalt carry me out of Mitzrayim and bury me in their burying place.

And Yisrael bowed down. He payed homage to Yosef because he held royal position. However, I believe it means he bowed to God in praise. Our verse is different from the verse which records the bowing of Avraham (Bereshit 23:7), for in the latter case it is explicitly stated that Avraham bowed to the children of Chet.
That one said to Yosef. Someone said to Yosef. Whom she bore to Levi in Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 26:59) is similar.
And one told Yaakov. Someone told Yaakov. Or it may refer to the one who said to Yosef, Behold, thy father is sick. On the other hand, he may have been a messenger sent by Yaakov.

[Behold, I will make thee fruitful.] According to Saadiah Gaon Yaakov told Yosef: Hashem appeared to me and told me, Behold I will make thee fruitful. However, following this promise I had no other children, and Rachel died. I now know that the Divine promise of Behold, I will make thee fruitful was said concerning your children. This interpretation is totally unpalatable. What difference is there between Yosef’s children and Reuven’s children? Furthermore, Binyamin was born after this prophetic vision. I believe that Yaakov told Yosef the following: “Hashem appeared to me and told me that the land of Kenaan will be an everlasting possession for my children. I now give you a first born’s share in this land. Therefore let Efraim and Menashe share in the land in the same manner as Reuven and Shimon, my two eldest sons (v. 5). However, any children that will be born to you in addition to Efraim and Menashe shall be called after the name of their just noted brothers, namely, they will receive their inheritance among them (v. 6). I take issue with the one who interprets And thy issue, that thou begettest after them (v. 6) as referring to the children of Machir the son of Menashe who were born upon Yosef’s knees (Bereshit 50:23). If his interpretation is correct, why does Scripture say, they shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance (v. 6)? And what if one argues, but we do not find that Yosef had any other children after Menashe and Efraim? It is not convincing. It is quite possible that Yosef had additional children but they are not mentioned because they received their inheritance among their brothers. There are many other such instances in Scripture.

[And as for me, when I came from paddan.] Rachel died suddenly and I was not able to transport her to the cave of Machpelah and inter her there, as I did with Leah. Yaakov told this to Yosef so that he would not be angry with him for requesting that he do for him what he didn’t do for his mother.

[And Yisrael beheld Yosef’s sons.] After stating in our verse, And Yisrael beheld Yosef’s sons, how could Scripture go on to say, Now the eyes of Yisrael were dim for age, so that he could not see (v. 10)? The answer is, so that he could not see means he was not able to see clearly and recognize their faces.
[I had not thought.] Pillalti (I thought) means, my mind never judged that I would ever see you. It comes from the same root as pelilim (judges) (Devarim 32:31).
And Yosef brought them out from between his knees. This verse should have followed And he blessed them that day, etc. (v. 20).
[From between his knees.] Yaakov sat on the edge of the bed.
And Yosef took them both. Its meaning is: And Yosef had taken them both. I have already noted many other such instances.
Guiding his hands wittingly. His hands, as it were, understood what he wanted to do.

For Menashe was the first-born. Even though (ki) Menashe was the first-born. The word ki in O Lord, let the Lord…go in the midst of us, even though (ki) it is a stiff-necked people (Shemot 34:9) is similar. There are many similar instances.
[The angel who hath redeemed me.] The meaning of this will be found in the Torah portion Ve-eleh shemot (Shemot 23:20).

And let my name be named in them. All of Yisrael will be called Efraim and Yosef. Scripture also states, A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children; she refuseth to be comforted for her children, Because they are not (Yirmiyahu 31:15), because Yaakov considered Rachel to be his true mate. Hence Scripture says, The sons of Rachel Yaakov’s wife (Bereshit 46:19). Similarly, as soon as Rachel bore a son, Yaakov said to Lavan, Send me away, that I may go unto mine own place, and to my country (Bereshit 30:25). He also gave the birthright to Yosef because he was the first born of his true mate. When Reuven showed himself unfit for the birthright he transferred it to Yosef who was Rachel’s first born, rather than to Dan or Gad because they were sons of the handmaidens. [17. HIS RIGHT HAND.] The right hand is more honored and is stronger than the left.
A multitude of nations. Many nations shall descend from him
By thee shall Yisrael bless. All Bnei Yisrael.
And he set Efraim before Menashe. In the enunciation of the blessing.
One portion. Some say that shekhem (portion) alludes to the city of Shechem which was in the portion of the land allotted to Yosef.

With my sword and with my bow refers to Hashem, as in David’s statement, The lord is my rock…My shield and my horn of salvation (Tehillim 18:3; Shmuel II 22:3). However, I believe that shekhem means a portion and shekhem echad is to be rendered one portion. The word shekhem is related to the words shikhmam (their shoulders) and shekhem (shoulder) in, upon their shoulders (shichmam) (Shemot 12:34), and To serve Him with one consent (shekhem echad) (Tzefanyah 3:9).
Above thy brethren. More than thy brethren.

[Which I took.] Its meaning is: which Bnei Yisrael will take with their sword and with their bow. Yaakov singled out the Emori because there were none among the seven Kenaani nations equal in strength to them. Observe, after the two mighty Emori kings were slain Yehoshua said (Yehoshua 7:7), Alas, O Hashem Hashem, wherefore hast Thou at all brought this people over the Yarden, to deliver us into the hand of the Emori, to cause us to perish? Yaakov’s statement, Which I took, presents no problems because the Patriarchs considered the land as theirs from the moment that Hashem verbally gave it to Avraham. Hashem similarly gave it to Yaakov, as we read, The land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed (Bereshit 28:13).

That which shall befall you. Prophecies foretelling that which shall befall you in the future. Those who base themselves on Scripture’s closing remark, and this is that their father spoke unto them and blessed them (v. 28), and conclude that they (Yaakov’s words) are blessings, err. For if it were so, where are the blessings of Reuven, Shimon and Levi? The way to understand and this is that their father spoke unto them and blessed them is as follows: and this (v. 3-27) is what their father spoke unto them by way of prophecy after which he blessed them. Scripture omits the blessings.

Reuven, thou art my first-born, my might, and the first-fruits of my strength. My might was first seen in thee. The first-born is called the first of one’s strength. We find an identical expression in And smote all the first-born in Mitzrayim, The first-fruits of their strength in the tents of Cham (Tehillim 78:51).
The excellency of dignity. You were suited by virtue of being first-born for the advantage of being exalted above all your brothers.
And the excellency of power. This means the same as The excellency of dignity. It is prophetic style to repeat the same idea in different words. The meaning of oz is power.
Unstable. Because you acted unstably as water does.

Have not thou the excellency. (Some say) that al totar (have not thou the excellency) means, you will not have the advantage. However, if this were the case then our text should have read al tutar rather than al totar; i.e., the vav of totar should have been vocalized with a shuruk. Others say that our clause should be interpreted thus: you acted unstably as water that is poured out of a vessel and you gained nothing thereby (al totar). However, I disagree with this interpretation. The term al is always used in Scripture as an imperative. The latter fact is not negated by the fact that we find al used once in a non-imperative sense in In the way of righteousness is life, And in the pathway thereof there is no (al) death (Mishlei 12:28). The correct translation of our clause is: do not seek any advantage (al totar) even one as insignificant as water. Accordingly the vav of totar is properly vocalized with a cholam, and it follows the paradigm of tosaf (more) in Think upon the battle, thou wilt do so no more (al tosaf) (Iyov 40:32). Rabbi Saadiah Gaon explains our line as follows: you will not have any advantage over your brothers even one as insignificant as water. According to Saadiah pachaz (unstable) comes from the same root as pochazim (light, insignificant) in vain and light (pochazim) fellows (Shoftim 9:4), and the root of the word pachaz does not have to be inverted.

Then defiledst thou it. From the day that thou defiled my couch, my conjugal couch was removed. Yetzu’i alah (he went up to my couch) is to be interpreted as if written yetzu’i alah me’alai (my conjugal couch went up from me). Furthermore, the word alah (went up) at times has the meaning of cut off, as in O my God, take me not away (al ta’aleni) in the midst of my days (Tehillim 102:25). Our chapter is clearly explained in Chronicles where we read, Reuven (was) the first-born of Yisrael…but, forasmuch as he defiled his father’s couch, his birthright was given unto the sons of Yosef the son of Yisrael, and he was not to be reckoned in the genealogy as first-born (Divrei Hayamim I 5:1). Chronicles then tells us that Yosef received the birthright and Yehudah the kingship (Ibid. v. 2). Some explain that and he was not to be reckoned in the genealogy as first-born means that the listing of the order of the twelve sons would start with Reuven.
Shimon and Levi are brethren. He referred to them as brethren because of what they did to the city of Shechem.

Their kinship. Some say that the word mekherotehem (their kinship) is similar in meaning to ha-karat (the show of) in The show of (ha-karat) their countenance doth witness against them (Is. 3:9). However, this interpretation is grammatically impossible. Others say that mekherotehem is to be rendered their possessions and is to be compared to the word tikhru (ye shall buy) in and ye shall also buy (tikhru) water of them for money (Devarim 2:6). However, this, too, is incorrect for the word tikhru means to dig. Others say that mekherotehem is related to the word mekhirah (sale) and the meaning of mekherotehem is they sold themselves, as in a people that jeoparded (cheref) their lives unto the death (Jud. 5:18). I believe that mekherotehem comes from the same root as mekhorotayich (thine origin) (Yechezkel 16:3). While the prepositional bet is missing from mekherotehem, we find the same with the word bet (house) in that was found in the house of (bet) Hashem (Melachim II 16:8) and with the word ma’on (habitation) in which I have commanded in My habitation (ma’on) (Shmuel I 2:29). Our text refers to the violence which Shimon and Levi committed in the land of their origin by deceitfully slaying the entire city of Shechem after making a covenant with them.

Let my soul not come into their council. Rabbi Aharon explained the word tavo (come) in Let my soul not come (tavo) as having the meaning of set like the meaning of ba (goeth down, to set) in and the sun goeth down (ba) (Kohelet 1:5). He interpreted let my soul not come into their council as meaning, I do not want to be outside of their council. However, Rabbi Aharon’s interpretation inverts the meaning of the verse. If Yaakov praised Shimon and Levi, why did he mention weapons of violence? Furthermore, Yaakov told his sons, Ye have troubled me, to make me odious unto the inhabitants of the land (Bereshit 34:30). The truth of the matter is that Shimon and Levi placed Yaakov and his household in great jeopardy by their actions in Shechem. Indeed, were it not for the terror of Elokim that was upon the cities that were round about them (Bereshit 35:5), they would have surrounded Yaakov and his family and exterminated them all. He (Rabbi Aharon) similarly explained Cursed be their anger (v. 7) as meaning and in their self will they uprooted a cursed wall, for their anger was fierce. The above explanations are unpalatable. Let my soul not come into their council. Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that kevodi (my glory) is synonymous with nafshi (my soul). He notes that we find the two often used synonymously in the book of Tehillim. Rabbi Moshe’s interpretation is correct since our text repeats itself in different words, as is the style of prophetic statements. We thus find, Ask thy father, and he will declare unto thee, Thine elders, and they will tell thee (Devarim 32:7), and (in Bamidbar 23:8) How shall I curse, whom Elokim hath not cursed? And how shall I execrate, whom the Lord hath not execrated? Thus into their council means the same as unto their assembly, come (tavoh) the same as be united (techad), and nafshi the same as kevodi. However, Rabbi Yehudah ben Balam the Spaniard says that Rabbi Moshe erred. He maintains that kavod (glory) refers to the body because the body is the glory (kavod) of the soul in the same way that a necklace is the ornament to the neck, as we find in the verse Who satisfieth thy body (edyekh) with good things (Tehillim 103:5). Rabbi Yehudah offers as a proof text, Yea, let him lay my glory (kevodi) in the dust. Selah. (Tehillim 7:6). However, I say that Rabbi Yehudah errs, for we find Scripture saying, So that my glory (kevodi) may sing praise to Thee (Tehillim 30:13), and Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory (kevodi) rejoiceth; My flesh (i.e., my body) also dwelleth in safety (Tehillim 16:9). As to the proof which Rabbi Yehudah offered from Yea, let him lay my glory in the dust, it is figurative. What the verse means is that my soul will be lowered as low as possible, i.e., to the dust. Positive proof that my interpretation is correct comes from My soul (nafshi) cleaveth unto the dust (Tehillim 119:25).

Be united. Techad (be united) is related to the word yachad (united). However, according to Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen, the grammarian of blessed memory, the tzere beneath the tav of techad takes the place of the alef of echad. He similarly explains the word tesham (be desolate) in and that the land be not desolate (tesham) (Bereshit 47:19).

[Into their council.] Be-sodam (into their council) is analogous to be-hivvasedam (while they took council) in while they took council (be-hivvasedam) together against me (Tehillim 31:14). The meaning of our verse is: since Shimon and Levi’s weapons are ones of violence (v. 5), Let my soul not come into their council.

They slew men. Scripture employs the term ish (man) generically as it does shor (ox) and chamor (ass) for oxen and asses (Bereshit 32:6). They slew men alludes to the inhabitants of the city of Shechem.
Oxen. Shor (oxen) is to be rendered as wall. We similarly read, Its branches run over the wall (shur) (v. 22). I have already explained in my work Moznayim that the cholam and shuruk interchange.
[Houghed.] Ikkeru (houghed) is similar to the word te’akker (hough) in thou shalt hough (te’akker) their horses (Yehoshua 11:6). This verse shows that Shechem was a large city since it had a wall.

Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce. Yaakov either prophesied or offered a prayer that Shimon and Levi’s anger would (or should) diminish and that this would be for their very own good. For curse is the opposite of bless, and as a blessing means an increase, so a curse means a diminution.

And their wrath. A repetition in different words of their anger. The same is true with I will divide them and And scatter them. The meaning of I will divide them in Yaakov, And scatter them in Yisrael is, Shimon and Levi deserve to be separated and disunited. And so it was. For we find that the lot of the tribe of Shimon fell within the inheritance of the tribe of Yehudah. Shimon was thus under Yehudah’s dominion. Furthermore, its cities were discontiguous and scattered throughout the boundary of Yehudah. Similarly the forty-eight cities of the tribe of Levi were scattered among the other tribes.

Yehudah. Thou art as thy name, and thy brethren shall so praise thee. When thy brothers shall see that Thy hand shall be on the neck of thine enemies; Thy father’s sons shall bow down before thee as to a king. This prophecy came to pass.

Yehudah is a lion’s whelp. Yaakov compared Yehudah to a small lion’s whelp, to a type of whelp that grows into a lion. The comparative caf (meaning like) has been omitted, as it is in When a wild ass’s colt (ayir pere) is born a man (Iyov. 11:12).

From the prey, my son, thou art gone up. My son, you appear to me as a lion’s whelp when thou art gone up from the prey. From the prey means after tearing a prey apart. This is its plain meaning. For us to interpret it as referring to the saving of Yosef, Scripture should have written he’elita (thou brought up) rather than alita (thou art come up) which is an intransitive verb. The rest of the verse is proof that the first part of the verse deals with Yehudah’s tearing of a prey and not with Yehudah’s saving of Yosef from being a prey. Observe the verse And she brought up (va-ta’al) one of her whelps (Yechezkel 19:3).
[He stooped down, he couched as a lion.] After a lion tears its prey it sits on its knees and couches in security and no other passing animal will cause it to get up and flee.

The sceptre shall not depart from Yehudah. The sceptre of greatness shall not depart from Yehudah until David, who inaugurated the Kingdom of Yehudah, comes. And so it was. Observe that in Yisrael’s march toward the promised land, the standard of the tribe of Yehudah set forth in the first (Bamidbar 10:14). Hashem also said, Yehudah shall go up first (Jud. 1:1, 2).
[Nor the ruler’s staff.] A scribe (mechokek) who will write (she-yachok) in a book.
[From between his feet.] Scribes sit at the feet of the ruler.

Shiloh. Some interpret Shiloh as Onkelos does. They say that it means “his.” Others say that Shiloh comes from the same root as u-ve-shilyatah (and against her afterbirth) (Devarim 28:57). Others connect it to the Rabbinic term shalil (embryo). There is also a commentator who says that shiloh refers to the city Shilo. He would explain yavo to mean goeth down, as in and the sun goeth down (ba) (Kohelet 1:5). Or he would maintain that our verse is abridged and should read as if written ad ki yavo ketz shilo (until the end of Shiloh comes). For it is written, And he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh (Tehillim 78:60), and then, He chose David also His servant (Tehillim 78:70). The latter interpretation is also not implausible. It is also possible that Shiloh means his son, with the heh taking the place of the vav, as in the word oholoh (his tent) (Bereshit 9:21), and that the word shiloh comes from the same root as tashleh (give birth) in lo tashleh oti (don’t cause me to give birth) (Melachim II 4:28).

[Obedience.] The word yikkehat (obedience of) is similar to the word li-kehat in to obey (li-kehat) his mother (Mishlei 30:17). The yod of yikkehat is a third person imperfect prefix. The meaning of ve-lo yikkehat ammim is that nations shall obey him. Yaakov’s prophecy came true, for we find that many nations were subservient to David and his son Shlomo. Our phrase (v. 10) does not mean that the sceptre shall depart from Yehudah when David comes. Our verse may be compared to someone saying, so and so will not lack bread until the time that he will have many vineyards and fields. For I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of, viz., returning you to the land of Kenaan (Bereshit 28:15), is identical.

Binding. The yod of oseri (binding) is superfluous. It is similar to the superflous yods of ha-yoshevi (that are enthroned) (Tehillim 123:1) and le-susati (to a steed) (Cant. 1:9) both of which are superfluous.
His foal. Iroh (his foal) is similar to ayarim (ass colts) in on thirty ass colts (ayarim) (Jud. 10:4).

The yod of beni (colt) in beni atono (his ass’s colt) is superfluous. The meaning of our verse then is: Binding his foal unto the vine and binding his ass’s colt unto the choice vine, for the word binding is to be read as if written twice.
Unto the choice vine. Scripture repeats the same idea in different words, for sorekah (vine) means the same as gefen, and ayir (foal) the same as aton.

Similarly, And his vesture in the blood of grapes. Some say that suto (his vesture) is the word kesuto (his vesture) with the kaf missing. However, I believe that sutoh comes from the same root as masveh (veil) (Shemot 34:33). The meaning of our verse is that his vineyards will produce so many grapes that Yehudah will bind his foal to the vine and he will not care if the animal eats of the grapes; and he will have so much wine that he will wash his garments in wine rather than in water. Scripture terms wine the blood of grapes because wine is red. The Bible speaks figuratively here, as it does in And it shall come to pass in that day, That the mountains shall drop down sweet wine, And the hills shall flow with milk (Yoel 4:18). The land will produce so much wine that Yehudah will be called “red eyes” because of the great amount of wine that he will drink. He will be so called because the eyes of one who drinks much wine look red. Similarly Yehudah’s teeth will be white from the large amount of milk that he will drink.

And his teeth white. U-leven (white) is an adjective modifying shinnayim (teeth). Shinnayim is in the dual form because the teeth are arranged in two sets. Saadiah Gaon, of blessed memory, explains His eyes shall based with wine to mean that his eyes shall be redder than wine. He similarly explains And his teeth white with milk to mean that his teeth shall be whiter than milk. Others say that And his teeth white with milk means that he will not eat an unclean thing and will not follow what his eyes see. The latter is a ridiculous homily.
Yaakov at first enumerated the tribes in the order of their birth. However, he listed Zevulun before Yissachar because Yissachar’s inheritance fell between Zevulun and Dan.

At the shore of the sea. This, too, is proof that Yaakov prophesied. The meaning of le-chof (at the shore) is, at the border of. It comes from the same root as chofef (covereth) in He covereth (chofef) him all the day (Devarim 33:12). The border of the sea is called chof because it “covers” the boats as boats cannot be anchored in places that are open to the wind.
And his flank shall be upon Zidon. His flank shall extend to Zidon.
Yissachar is a large-boned ass. Yaakov compared Yissachar to an ass whose bones are heavy. Chamor (ass) is in the construct with garem (bones). Due to the heaviness of his bones, he is wont to couch.

Between the sheepfolds. Ben ha-mishpatayim (between the sheepfolds) means between the arranged rows. It is possible that mishpatayim comes from the same root as tishpot (arrange) in Hashem, Thou wilt arrange (tishpot) peace for us (Is. 26:12).

For he saw a resting-place that it was good. When Yissachar saw that his land and resting-place were pleasant, he, as an ass, bowed his shoulder to bear any and all burdens and became as a servant that pays levies. Scripture says this concerning Yissachar because this tribe did not consist of warriors and its men did not want to leave their homes to go to war. Moshe similarly said concerning Yissachar, Rejoice…Yissachar, in thy tents (Devarim 33:18). The levy mentioned in our verse may refer to Yissachar’s payment of a money levy to the king in Yisrael in lieu of furnishing soldiers for his army, or it may refer to a payment of money to foreign nations that they should not attack them.

Dan shall judge his people. Yaakov hinted that Dan, although born of a handmaid, would have a standard just as the tribes born of the wives did. Dan was thus a ruler over all the other tribes that were descended from the handmaids.

[A serpent.] Yaakov compared Dan in his strength to a serpent. It is also possible that shefifon (a horned snake) comes from the same root as yeshufekha (they shall bruise thy) in they shall bruise thy (yeshufekha) head (Bereshit 3:15). According to this interpretation shefifon ale orach (a horned snake in the path) means the same as nachash ale derech (a serpent in the way).

[I wait for thy salvation, o Hashem.] When the serpent bites the horse’s heel, it is afraid that the rider will smash its head with his sword. Hence the prophet prayed, I wait for Thy salvation, O Hashem. The “thy” of Thy salvation refers to Dan. The meaning of our verse is: I trust to Hashem for thy salvation. It is also possible that Scripture employs a noun (salvation) in place of an infinitive. Our verse should thus be rendered: I trust that Hashem will save thee. Thy salvation in We will shout for joy in thy salvation (Tehillim 20:6) is similar. The aforementioned is the case whether the “thy” of thy salvation (Tehillim 20:6) refers to King David or to the anointed, his son. Rabbi Shmuel Ha-Nagid says that the word va-yomer has been omitted from our clause and it should be read as if written: and he will say (va-yomer), I wait for Thy salvation, O Hashem. Rabbi Yitzchak explains our verse as follows: when the prophet Yaakov prophetically saw his son Dan in the form of a serpent, he was overtaken by fright and exclaimed, “Save me, O Hashem.”
Gad. Yaakov prophesied that a troop (an army) would attack Gad but that he would ultimately be victorious.

Shall troop upon him. Yegudennu (shall troop upon him) is similar to yegudennu (he invadeth) in the people that he invadeth (yegudennu) (Chavakuk 3:16). Yagud (he shall troop), like gedud (a troop), comes from the root gimel, dalet, dalet. It is vocalized with a shuruk in place of a cholam like the word yarun (doth sing) in But the righteous doth sing (yarun) and rejoice (Mishlei 29:6). We do not know exactly to what incident Yaakov was referring because we don’t know all the tribulations that our ancestors endured.

As for Asher. Some say that the mem of me-asher (as for Asher) is superfluous. However, I believe that what our clause means is: from the land of Asher “fat bread” will come. Bread in our verse is in the feminine. We find the same to be the case with the words house, place, hand, fire, eye, wind, land, chest and people.
[Royal dainties.] The meaning of ma’adanne melekh (royal dainties) is known. Moshe similarly said concerning Asher, And let him dip his foot in oil (Devarim 33:24).

Naftali is a hind let loose. The word sheluchah (let loose) means a gift, and the one who receives such a gift responds with goodly words. Others say that hind refers to Devorah and that He giveth goodly words alludes to Barak who joined her in a song to God. Scripture mentions Naftali because Barak came from the tribe of Naftali.

Yosef is a fruitful vine. Ben means a branch and it is a feminine noun. Ben in And the branch (ben) that Thou madest strong for Thyself (Tehillim 80:16) has a similar meaning. Grammatically speaking porat (fruitful) is a po’elet. A feminine singular participle can come in two paradigms, viz., oyevah and oyevet, and similarly porah and porat. The word porat is related to the word poriyyah (fruitful) (Tehillim 128:3). There is a commentator who connects porat to the word porot (branches) in And brought forth branches (porot) (Yechezkel 17:6). The Bible repeats the phrase ben porot twice in succession, for that is Hebrew style. Compare, For, lo, Thine enemies, O Hashem, For, lo, Thine enemies shall perish (Tehillim 92:10). The repetition of a phrase indicates permanence. According to the second quoted interpretation a tav has been substituted for a heh as in the case of the tav of ve-shavat (then it shall return) in then it shall return (ve-shavat) to the prince (Yechezkel 46:17).

[Its branches run over the wall.] Yosef was as a fruitful vine. He gave birth to branches, each one of which ran over the wall; i.e., the branches were so tall that they ran over fortified walls. Scripture here combines banot (branches) with tza’adah (run) in a manner similar to Dead flies (zevuve) make the ointment of the perfumer fetid (yavish) (Kohelet 10:1).

Have dealt bitterly with him. Rabbi Shmuel Ha-Nagid explains this verse as meaning: they set his gall for a target (va-yemareruhu) and then the archers shot at him (va-robbu). The word rabbim (archers) in Call together the archers (rabbim) against Bavel, All them that bend the bow (Yirmiyahu 50:29) is similar to va-robbu in our verse. His archers compass me round about…He poureth out my gall upon the ground (Iyov 16:13) is similar to our verse.
And hated him. First they hated him and then they set up his gall as a target. We must thus explain va-yistemuhu to mean, and they had hated him.

Logically, va-yistemuhu should come first, i.e., the sequence should be they hated him, they set his gall as a target, and they shot at thim. Hence va-yistemuhu should be taken as a pluperfect (Weiser). This alludes to Yosef’s brothers who sold him into slavery.
But his bow abode firm. His bow abode in a firm place.

Were made supple. Va-yafozzu means, and they strengthened themselves. I believe that va-yafozzu comes from the same root as mefazzez (leaping) (Shmuel II 6:16). There are those who connect va-yafozzu to the word paz (pure gold). However, their interpretation makes no sense.

The meaning of our text (v. 23 and 24) is that the archers hated Yosef and gathered together to spill his gall. However, his adversaries were afraid of him because his bow and hands were strong. They therefore could not overcome him.

By the hands of the mighty one of Yaakov. From thence. The Mighty One of Yaakov alludes to Hashem. From the power that Yosef received from the Mighty One of Yaakov he was able to become, and indeed became, “the shepherd of the stone of Yisrael.” And so it was, for we read, And Yosef sustained his father, and his brethren, and all his father’s household, with bread (Bereshit 47:12). Yaakov employed the term Mighty One of Yaakov for Hashem because Hashem knew of his deep love for Yosef.

The meaning of stone is the very thing. Some say that mi-sham (from thence) should be interpreted from that time. However, we never find the word sham (there) to have this meaning anywhere in Scripture. This commentator also interprets the Shepherd, the Stone of Yisrael as meaning: the one whose heart died and was as stone, but who revived to feed (ro’eh), i.e., to live by eating. However, this interpretation is farfetched.

Even by the Hashem of thy father. I believe that this verse is connected to the preceding one. Its meaning is: the power which you possess came to you from the Hashem of thy father, who shall help thee. The mem of me-el (even by Hashem) is also to be prefixed to ve-et (and by). The mem of me-el is like the bet of be-el (as Hashem) (Shemot 6:3) which is also to be prefixed to u-ve-shemi (but by my name). Thus And from the Almighty, who shall bless thee repeats the idea contained in From the Hashem of thy father, who shall help thee. Saadiah Gaon explains the phrase me-el avikha to mean, I will ask of the Hashem of thy fathers. It is possible that With blessings of heaven above is connected to, From the Hashem of thy father. The meaning of our text is explained by They (the blessings) shall be on the head of Yosef, And on the crown of the prince among his brethren (v. 26).

Blesssings of the deep. Moshe similarly said, And for the precious things of the earth and the fullness thereof (Devarim 33:13). The word tehom (the deep) is feminine both in our verse and in Devarim (33:16). It is similarly feminine in The deep (tehom) made it to grow (Yechezkel 31:4). The meaning of With blessings of heaven above, Blessings of the deep that coucheth beneath is that rain will descend from the heavens above upon the land of Yosef and that the deep which coucheth beneath the earth will fill its rivers and springs with an abundance of water.

Blessings of the breasts, and of the womb. Yaakov likened the breasts to heaven and the womb to the earth, its meaning being that Yosef will be blessed with many children. The opposite of this blessing is the curse, Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts (Hoshea 9:14).
The blessings of thy father. These blessings which I have blessed you with are mighty and are added to the blessing with which my progenitors blessed me.

[Progenitors.] Horai is to be rendered my begetters. Va-tahar (and she gave birth to) in and she gave birth to (va-tahar) Miriam (Divrei Hayamim I 4:17) and horah (brought forth) in, A man-child is brought forth (horah) (Iyov 3:3) are similar.

Unto the utmost bound. Ta’avat (utmost bound of) comes from the same root as ve-hitavvitem (and ye shall mark out your line) (Bamidbar 34:10). The meaning of our verse is: these blessings will be as high as the line marked out by the everlasting hills.

The prince among his brethren. Nezir (prince of) comes from the same root as nezer (crown). It is in the construct with echav (his brethren) and is therefore vocalized nezir. Compare, nediv lev (willing-hearted) (Shemot 35:22).
Binyamin. Yaakov compared Binyamin to a wolf because Binyamin was mighty. The men of Givah are proof of this.

The prey. Ad (the prey) has the same meaning as the Aramaic word for spoil (ada). Similarly, ad in Then is the prey (ad) of a great spoil divided (Is. 33:23) and in Until the day that I rise up to the prey (ad) (Tzefanyah 3:8); and iddim (a polluted garment) (Is. 64:5)..

[And at even he divideth.] At even he divideth among his children the prey that he has taken as spoil. Yehoshua says that our verse alludes to King Shaul who defeated the Amaleki. He explains In the morning as alluding to the beginning of Yisrael’s kingdom and at even as referring to the period of Yisrael’s exile with regard to Mordechai. However, this interpretation is the way of the Midrash. Onkelos’ interpretation of our verse is well known.

Every one according to his blessing. The blessing which Yaakov gave each one of his sons came to pass upon each one. The meaning of every one according to his blessing is similar in meaning to each man according to the interpretation of his dream (Bereshit 41:11).
And he charged them. He (Yaakov) charged that all should go along with Yosef to bury him.

He gathered up his feet into the bed. Until then he had been sitting on the bed with his feet dangling over its edge as is contemporarily the custom in Christian communities. The beds in Moslem countries are constructed differently from the beds in Christian countries.

And the physicians embalmed Yisrael. They powdered his body with a preservative. It is possible, though a bit far fetched, that chanetah (putteth forth) in The fig-tree putteth forth (chanetah) her green figs (Cant. 2:13) is analogous to va-yechantu (embalmed).
Which I have digged. Kariti means I have digged. Kariti is similar to yikhreh in if a man shall dig (yikhreh) a pit (Shemot 21:33).
And with him went up all the servants of Paroh. All of Mitzrayim with the exception of Yosef are called servants of Paroh.
[Chariots. The word rechev (chariot) is similar in meaning to mirkevet (chariot).
Horsemen. The meaning of parashim (horsemen) is well-known.]
And he made a mourning for his father seven days. This, as our sages of blessed memory say, took place after they interred Yaakov.
And his sons did unto him. That is: And behold his sons did as he commanded them, namely, carried him and buried him in the place that he commanded them to inter him.

It may be that Yosef will hate us. Perhaps Yosef will harbor a hatred for us. Yistemenu (will hate us) is analogous to va-yistom in And Esav hated (va-yistom) Yaakov (Bereshit 27:41). The word lu (it may be) is used in Scripture in many ways.
I pray thee. Anna (I pray thee) is a conciliatory expression.
[For am I in the place of Elokim.] Saadiah Gaon explains this as meaning: am I in the place of Elokim that you fall before my face and say, Behold, we are thy bondmen?
To pass. Aso (to pass) is an infinitive.
Children of the third generation. In view of the fact that bene (children of) is in the construct with shilleshim (third), the children referred to are the fourth generation.
Were born. Yulledu (were born) means grew up.
And they embalmed him. The physicians.

And he was put in a coffin. Someone put him in a coffin. The root of va-yisem is yod, sin, mem and follows the paradigm of va-yitzer (formed) (Bereshit 2:7). However, Rabbi Yonah, the grammarian, says that va-yisem is vocalized with a chirik in place of a shuruk. However, I consider this interpretation to be far-fetched.
[In a coffin.] The reason why ba-aron (in a coffin) is vocalized with a kamatz is that it signifies the coffin which he had prepared for himself.
